sentences.text: The evidence is mixed: in-flight oral endotracheal intubation by flight nurses on a manikin took significantly longer than on an emergency department stretcher, but correct tracheal placement was not significantly worse. In a BO-105 helicopter, flight nurses performed three manikin intubations in each setting (in-flight vs ED stretcher). Mean in-flight time was 25.9 +/- 10.9 seconds versus 13.2 +/- 2.8 seconds in the control setting (ANOVA F=38.7, p<.001). All control intubations were correctly placed in the trachea, while in-flight had two (6.7%) esophageal intubations, but this difference was not significant (chi2=0.3; p>0.05).
The evidence is mixed: a dedicated discharge coordinator improved some aspects of discharge quality but not others.

In an intervention study of 600 randomly sampled adults discharged home from three medical wards, quality of discharge planning was assessed before and after introducing a district discharge planning policy/checklist and then a discharge coordinator over three phases spanning 18 months.

After the discharge coordinator was introduced, the discharge planning process improved, patients had fewer problems after discharge, and they reported less perceived need for medical and healthcare services, but there was no evidence of more timely or effective community services or improved appropriateness/efficiency of bed use.
No, the Barthel Index alone does not appear to be an adequate measure of long-term outcome after stroke, because its correlations with other outcome dimensions are highly variable and sometimes weak.

In 106 interviewed survivors of first-ever stroke (median age 71, mean follow-up 4.9 years) in south east London, Barthel scores correlated strongly with physical functioning (r=0.810) and Frenchay activities (r=0.826), but weakly with SF36 role emotional (r=0.217), life satisfaction (r=0.361), and not significantly with Nottingham health profile sleep (r=-0.189, NS).
This suggests that the Barthel Index captures physical disability but misses important quality-of-life, emotional, and participation domains.
Yes—low serum chloride was associated with higher cardiovascular mortality in a 10-year cohort.

In 4793 men and 4313 women aged 25-74 years who were free of symptomatic coronary heart disease at baseline, serum chloride level was one of the strongest predictors of cardiovascular disease mortality independently of age, body mass index, sex, smoking, systolic blood pressure, cholesterol levels, uric acid, creatinine, total proteins, and diuretic intake.

For subjects with serum chloride ≤100 mmol/l compared with those above that limit, the adjusted risk ratio for cardiovascular disease death was 1.65 (95% CI 1.06-2.57) in men and 2.16 (95% CI 1.11-4.22) in women.
Adjusted risk ratios across four baseline serum chloride groups also showed a decreasing log-linear dose-response relation to total and cardiovascular mortality.

The evidence is mixed but suggestive that perforation of the appendix is a risk factor for tubal infertility and possibly ectopic pregnancy, based on a review reporting elevated risk estimates but weakened by bias and confounding. The review included 23 retrieved articles, of which only 4 presented original data with nonexposed control groups. It reported risk estimates ranging from 1.6 (95% CI 1.1 to 2.5) for ectopic pregnancy after appendectomy to 4.8 (95% CI 1.5 to 14.9) for tubal infertility from perforation of the appendix. However, recall bias and poor adjustment for confounding variables in some reports weakened the validity of these studies.
No, variations in the use of carotid endarterectomy were not explained by population need.

In two English health regions, utilisation varied 14-fold across district populations, but there was no association with district stroke mortality (r=-0.06, 95% CI -0.41 to 0.30) or stroke admission rates (r=0.17, 95% CI -0.2 to 0.49).
Instead, higher utilisation was strongly related to residence in districts where services were located, and rates were lowest in the most affluent wards.
Yes, the PET evidence supports that amoxapine has the receptor-occupancy profile of an atypical antipsychotic.

In seven healthy volunteers given 50–250 mg/day for 5 days, 5-HT2 receptors were near saturation at ≥100 mg/day, and D2 occupancy increased dose-dependently but never exceeded 80%, with 5-HT2 occupancy exceeding D2 occupancy at all doses.
These findings meet the stated atypical antipsychotic criteria of high 5-HT2 occupancy, greater 5-HT2 than D2 occupancy, and D2 occupancy not exceeding 80%.

Yes, laparoscopic reoperation for failed antireflux surgery appears feasible based on a case series of 46 consecutive patients. The study included patients with previous antireflux procedures (laparoscopic in 21, laparotomy in 21, thoracotomy in 3, thoracoscopy in 1). Laparoscopic reoperations were completed with a 20% overall conversion rate (0% in the last 10 patients), 0% mortality, mean hospital stay 2.3 days for completed laparoscopic cases, and 89% (31/35) satisfaction at follow-up. These results support feasibility, though as a case series without a comparison group, they do not establish superiority over open reoperation.

No, clinician assessment was not accurate enough in this study, resting on a physician sensitivity of only 39% for predicting acute chest syndrome. Among 73 patients with sickle cell disease and 96 febrile events (temperature at least 38°C) evaluated before chest radiography, 24% (23/96) had radiographic acute chest syndrome, but 61% (14/23) of those cases were not clinically suspected by the evaluating physician. No symptom or physical examination finding except splinting (4/23 versus 0/73) helped identify acute chest syndrome, 57% of acute chest syndrome patients had completely normal physical examinations, and diagnostic accuracy did not improve significantly with increasing pediatric training.

The evidence is insufficient to answer specifically for aortic surgery; in patients undergoing vascular surgery, desflurane did not alter left ventricular function when used to control surgical stimulation.
In 50 vascular surgery patients, 16 developed hypertension at incision and were given desflurane to return systolic arterial pressure to within 20% of post-induction values.

Desflurane restored afterload indices (systemic vascular resistance index, end-systolic wall stress, left-ventricular stroke work index) to post-induction values, with no change in heart rate, cardiac index, stroke volume, end-diastolic or end-systolic cross-sectional areas, fractional area change, or left ventricular circumferential fiber shortening.
No data are provided on aortic surgery specifically.
Yes, the Mammography Quality Standards Act (MQSA) was associated with improved mammography quality in North Carolina.
Among all mammography facilities inspected in 1993–1994 and again in 1995, the percentage meeting quality standards increased after MQSA implementation.
Phantom image passing rates rose from 31.6% to 78.2%, darkroom fog passing rates from 74.3% to 88.5%, and developer temperature difference passing rates from 62.4% to 86.9%.
Yes, the evidence suggests the NIHSS favors left hemisphere strokes because language deficits are weighted more heavily than neglect.
The NIHSS has 42 possible points, with 7 directly related to language compared with only 2 related to neglect.

In the placebo arm of the NINDS t-PA stroke trial, right hemisphere strokes had statistically greater infarct volumes than left hemisphere strokes after adjusting for baseline NIHSS (P<0.001), and for each 5-point NIHSS category below 20, median right-hemisphere volumes were about double left-hemisphere volumes.
For example, at a 24-hour NIHSS of 16 to 20, the median left-hemisphere infarct volume was 48 mL versus 133 mL for right-hemisphere strokes (P<0.001).
This means left hemisphere strokes can produce similar NIHSS scores with smaller infarcts, consistent with the scale favoring left-hemisphere deficits.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that prophylaxis in all hospitalised medical patients makes sense.
In a general internal ward, symptomatic venous thrombosis during hospitalisation occurred in 39/6332 patients (0.6%), a low overall incidence.
Risk was concentrated in patients with known malignancy: 24/876 (2.7%) versus 15/5456 (0.3%) in non-cancer patients, with a relative risk of 10.0 (95% CI 5.3–18.9).

The passage does not compare universal versus targeted prophylaxis, so it does not directly answer whether prophylaxis in all patients is warranted; it suggests targeting high-risk patients such as those with malignancy.

Yes, the evidence supports that hypotensive events can be followed by myocardial ischaemic events in patients with ischaemic heart disease, with 14 hypotension-induced ischaemic events occurring in 8 of 25 patients and ST events significantly associated with preceding hypotensive events (chi2=40.2, p<0.0001).
The study enrolled 25 patients with angina on one or more hypotensive cardiovascular medications and documented hypotension, recording 107 hypotensive events and 40 ST events in 14 patients.

Among the 14 hypotension-induced ischaemic events, 13 were preceded by a fall in diastolic pressure (median 57.5 mm Hg, IQR 11) and 6 by a fall in systolic pressure, and patients with these events were more often on multiple hypotensive drug regimens (8/8 vs 9/17, p=0.022).
Because this was an observational study, it demonstrates a strong temporal association but does not definitively prove causation.
No, the supplied study found no significant association between antiphospholipid antibodies and avascular necrosis of bone in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.
In a cohort of 265 SLE patients followed from 1978 to 1998, 11 had AVN, giving a point prevalence of 4%.

There were no significant differences in the presence of individual antiphospholipid antibodies (IgM or IgG anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant) or their combination between the AVN group and the two control groups.
Thus, this evidence does not support a role for aPL status as a risk factor for AVN, though the study was designed to investigate it with adjustment for corticosteroid use.
Yes, head positioning influences anterior chamber depth in pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

In 39 patients with clinically apparent unilateral pseudoexfoliation and elevated intraocular pressure, central anterior chamber depth in the pseudoexfoliation eyes decreased from a mean of 3.08 mm supine to 2.95 mm prone, while fellow eyes decreased from 3.01 mm to 2.97 mm.
The decrease in anterior chamber depth when facing down was significantly greater in the pseudoexfoliation eyes than in the fellow eyes.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that abdominal CT is always necessary in intoxicated blunt trauma patients.

In a study of 324 intoxicated blunt trauma patients with GCS 15 and unremarkable abdominal examination, 317 (98%) had negative CT scans, abdominal injuries were identified in 7 (2%), and only 2 (0.6%) required abdominal exploration.
A significant association was found between major chest injury and abdominal injury, but no comparison was made to a strategy of omitting CT.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that open access endoscopy closes the door to an adequately informed patient, although open access patients reported receiving significantly less information to help identify the procedure and less explanation about its nature than patients referred from a GI subspecialty clinic (p<0.01 and p<0.005, respectively).
The comparison was between outpatients presenting for upper and lower endoscopy referred via open access versus a GI subspecialty clinic.
The study did not directly measure adequacy of informed consent, and satisfaction was similar for conscious sedation but higher for GI clinic patients undergoing unsedated flexible sigmoidoscopy.
No, the supplied case-control study found no increased risk of bleeding complications in Werlhof's disease patients undergoing cardiac surgery with extracorporeal circulation.

In ten WD patients matched to five non-WD controls each, total mediastinal drainage loss was almost identical (1140 ml in WD vs 1197 ml in no-WD), and one patient in each group had a bleeding complication requiring reexploration.
WD patients did have significantly lower platelet counts and received more platelet concentrates (mean 2.3 vs 0.7, P=0.007), but this did not translate into more bleeding.

The evidence is insufficient to settle whether folic acid must be continued beyond 1 year, but it supports continuation for at least 1 year because stopping it increased toxicity. In 75 RA patients established on methotrexate <20 mg weekly and folic acid 5 mg daily, those randomized to placebo instead of continuing folic acid had more early study withdrawal (46% vs 21%, P=0.02), two discontinuations for neutropenia, and more nausea at 9 months (45% vs 7%, P=0.001). Placebo patients had lower disease activity on a few measures, but this was probably not clinically significant. Thus the trial shows harm from stopping folic acid over 1 year, but it does not directly establish requirements beyond that period.
No, this cross-sectional study does not support alexithymia as an overall risk factor for unexplained physical symptoms in general medical outpatients.

Among 321 internal medicine outpatients, 169 had medically unexplained symptoms after complete physical examinations, and although they more often had a mental disorder, overall they were not more alexithymic than patients with explained symptoms.

In patients with unexplained symptoms, alexithymia was not associated with subjective health experience or use of medical services, though a subgroup with both unexplained symptoms and a mental disorder who denied any emotional-physical connection did have more alexithymic traits.
Because the study was cross-sectional, it cannot establish alexithymia as a risk factor, and it mainly shows no overall association.

The evidence suggests yes: PVR in adults late after TOF repair may be performed too late, because right ventricular volumes and function did not improve after surgery and recovery of RVEF was unlikely when preoperative RVEF was already reduced.

In 25 consecutive adults with significant pulmonary regurgitation late after TOF repair, mean RVEDV, RVESV, and RVEF were unchanged after PVR (227.1 vs 214.9 mL, p=0.74; 157.4 vs 155.4 mL, p=0.94; 35.6% vs 34.7%, p=0.78).
Only 2 of 15 patients (13%) with preoperative RVEF <0.40 reached RVEF ≥0.40 postoperatively, versus 5 of 10 (50%) with preoperative RVEF ≥0.40 (p<0.001).
No—the APACHE II score at ICU admission in emergency surgical patients appears treatment-dependent and overpredicts mortality, so it is not a reliable marker of physiological impairment.

In 85 consecutive emergency surgical patients admitted to a surgical ICU in 1999, the mean APACHE II score at ICU admission was 24.2 ± 8.3, about 36% higher than the preoperative score of 17.8 ± 7.7 (P<.001), suggesting the score was affected by treatment.
The preoperative score predicted 34% mortality versus 32% observed, but the ICU-admission score predicted 50% mortality versus 32% observed (P=.02), indicating poor calibration at that time point.

In 40 patients staying at least 10 days in the ICU, APACHE II scores differed significantly between survivors and those who died on day 10 (P=.04), but this does not establish reliability for physiological impairment.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that antral follicle assessment is a better predictor than age and FSH, but it did independently predict IVF outcome after controlling for both.

In 224 patients, baseline antral follicle >6 versus ≤6 was associated with clinical pregnancy rates of 51% versus 19%, and this difference remained significant after controlling for patient age and basal FSH.
Cancellation rates were also higher with antral follicle ≤6 (33% vs.
1%) and were significantly increased with advancing maternal age, elevated basal FSH, and antral follicle ≤6.
No—visual loss from amblyopia is not necessarily permanent, because nine amblyopic eyes in a case series showed improved acuity.

Among 465 patients with age-related macular degeneration, 189 had at least two standardized exams, 12 had improvement in the eye unaffected by macular disease, and nine of those had a history of amblyopia.

By 12 months, mean improvement in the amblyopic eyes was 3.3 lines logMAR for distance and 1.9 lines for near acuity, generally occurring between 1 and 12 months and remaining stable over follow-up; this small AMD case series does not establish whether such improvement occurs in all amblyopia populations.

No, the evidence does not show that managed care enables more low-income persons to identify a usual source of care; high managed care penetration was associated with a lower likelihood for uninsured low-income persons.

In a nationally representative sample of 14,271 low-income persons, uninsured persons in high penetration areas had a usual source of care 54.8% of the time versus 62.2% in low penetration areas, and a usual physician 60% versus 72.8%.
Managed care had only marginal effects on having a usual source of care for privately insured and Medicaid beneficiaries.
Thus, the study shows no overall enabling effect and a negative association for the uninsured.
Yes.
The finding rests on episodes being consistent (all manic or all mixed) in significantly more patients than would be expected by chance.

Over an 11-year period, the observed distribution of 1,224 manic and mixed episodes in 241 patients with three or more entries in a community mental health center management information system was compared with an expected distribution from 1,000 random simulations.
The observed consistency exceeded chance, supporting that the manic/mixed episode distinction tends to run true over time.

The evidence is insufficient to determine whether patient position influences venous air embolism risk during liver surgery, because the only supplied study found no negative intraluminal pressure and no hepatic-to-central venous pressure gradient in any tested position.
In 10 patients during liver surgery, central and hepatic venous pressures were measured with the operating table horizontal, 20 degrees head-up, and 20 degrees head-down.

Absolute pressures were highest in the head-down and lowest in the head-up tilt, but no negative intraluminal pressure was recorded and no pressure gradient between hepatic and central venous levels was demonstrable in any position.
Although head-down tilt is generally believed to decrease the likelihood of venous air embolism, these pressure findings do not directly establish an effect on embolism risk.
Yes, this single retrospective study suggests outcome can be predicted from respiratory parameters in children with malignancy and ARDS.
In 17 children (aged 10.5 ± 5.1 years) with ARDS and malignancy, 6 (35.3%) survived, and sepsis syndrome was present in 70.6%.

Peak inspiratory pressure, positive end-expiratory pressure, and ventilation index values could distinguish outcome by day 3, while efficiency of oxygenation (PaO2/FIO2 and P(A-a)O2) related to outcome from day 8 after mechanical ventilation onset.
However, these findings come from a small retrospective chart review, so they do not establish a validated prediction model.
No, increasing nerve length within the treatment volume did not improve pain relief in trigeminal neuralgia radiosurgery.
In 87 patients with typical trigeminal neuralgia randomized to one versus two isocenters, pain relief was identical for one- and two-isocenter radiosurgery.

The actuarial complete pain relief rate was 67.7% ± 5.1%, and improved pain relief correlated with younger age (p = 0.025) and fewer prior procedures (p = 0.039), while complications correlated with the nerve length irradiated (p = 0.018).
Thus, greater nerve length did not improve efficacy and was associated with more complications.
Evidence is insufficient to show that aggressive polyvalent antivenin use itself causes serious acute side effects, but in this high-dose series serious reactions were rare.
Among 65 rattlesnake-bite patients who received antivenin (mean 12.0 ± 6.0 vials; 43/65 [66%] got ≥10 vials), acute side effects within 6 hours occurred in 12 (18%, 95% CI 10%-30%).
All but 1 were solely urticaria; the exception (2%, 95% CI 0%-8%) had a prior antivenin reaction and required a short course of IV epinephrine for blood pressure support, with no other complications.
The study did not compare aggressive versus less aggressive dosing, so it cannot directly establish whether aggressive use changes the risk of serious acute side effects.
The evidence is mixed: delay in transfer to a rehabilitation ward was associated with longer total hospital length of stay but not with discharge to a more dependent residence.
In an observational study of 455 patients aged over 75 years with fracture of the proximal femur, 58% were transferred to a rehabilitation ward.
Each day of delay in transfer was associated with an additional 0.64 days of total hospital length of stay (95% CI 0.23-1.05).

For discharge to a more dependent residence among transferred patients, only age predicted outcome, with people over 85 having a relative risk of 1.47 (95% CI 1.15-1.88) compared with younger patients, not delay.

No, the passages describe a severe systemic reaction to sulfasalazine in a 21-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis—characterized by eosinophilia, granulomatous enteritis, myelotoxicity, cholestatic hepatitis, and seizures—rather than Crohn's disease.
The population is this single 21-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis, and no comparison group or numerical data are reported.
The passages do not mention Crohn's disease or provide diagnostic criteria, so they are insufficient to establish that diagnosis.

No—clinical variables did not accurately predict pathologic radiographs during a first episode of wheezing, based on a study where only pretreatment oxygen saturation differed significantly between radiographic groups and the discriminant model identified only 15% of pathologic radiographs.

In a prospective convenience sample of children with a first episode of wheezing, 61 patients (9%) had pathologic radiographs, and clinical score, respiratory rate, and presence of rales before or after treatment were not significantly different between the pathologic and nonpathologic groups.
The discriminant analysis correctly predicted 90% of nonpathologic radiographs but only 15% of pathologic radiographs.
The evidence is insufficient to say whether rugby headgear prevents concussion.
The only supplied study surveyed attitudes, not concussion outcomes, among 63 players from four Canadian teams and their coaches.
It found that 62% of players believed headgear could prevent concussion, while only 33% of coaches were convinced.
Because no data compared concussion incidence with versus without headgear, these passages do not establish efficacy.
The evidence does not support hepatitis G virus or TT virus as major specific causes of cryptogenic chronic liver disease.

In 23 patients with cryptogenic chronic liver disease versus 40 with hepatitis C virus-related chronic liver disease, hepatitis G virus RNA was detected in 4/23 (17.4%) versus 6/40 (15%), a nonsignificant difference.

At least one marker of hepatitis G virus infection was present in 6/23 (26.1%) versus 16/40 (40%), also nonsignificant, and TT virus DNA was found in only 1 cryptogenic patient and 2 hepatitis C virus patients.

Demographic and clinical features, including liver histology, were comparable between hepatitis G virus-infected and uninfected subjects, while severe liver damage was more frequent in hepatitis C virus disease.
Yes, receipt of hospice care in nursing homes was associated with better management of daily pain near the end of life.

In a retrospective cohort of nursing home residents with daily pain near death, 51% of hospice residents versus 33% of nonhospice residents received regular treatment for daily pain, and after controlling for clinical confounders hospice residents were about twice as likely to receive regular treatment (adjusted OR = 2.08, 95% CI = 1.68-2.56).

Hospice residents were also less likely to receive no analgesics (15% vs 23%; OR = 0.57, 95% CI = 0.45-0.74) and less likely to receive analgesics not recommended by AMDA (21% vs 29%; OR = 0.65, 95% CI = 0.52-0.80).
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether escalation of the apical dose changes treatment outcome in beta-radiation of posterior choroidal melanomas with 106Ru plaques.
The purpose was to review the optimal apical dose prescription (100 vs.
160 Gy), but no comparison of dose levels is reported.
In 48 patients with uveal melanomas (median height 3.85 mm plus 1 mm sclera), the median apical dose was 120 Gy and median scleral dose was 546 Gy.
After 5.8 years, the 5-year overall survival was 90%, disease-specific survival was 92%, local control was 90%, 6% received a second ruthenium application, and 10% of eyes were enucleated.
These passages do not compare different apical dose levels or report outcomes by dose escalation, so they do not show whether escalating the apical dose alters outcome.

Yes, to some extent: in a retrospective series of 49 patients with sonographically proven subclavian steal syndrome, the side-to-side systolic blood pressure difference was significantly higher in patients with complete reversal or alternating vertebral artery flow than in those with systolic deceleration (P<.001).
The study screened 1860 records and found SSS in 51 studies/49 patients; waveform analysis showed complete reversal in 16 (31%), alternating flow in 24 (47%), and systolic deceleration in 11 (22%).

Thus a larger interarm systolic pressure difference tracked with more severe steal waveforms, but the passage does not report predictive accuracy or a threshold, so it supports an association rather than proving the difference can predict severity.
No, the evidence indicates these risk factors do not confer equal risk in women and men.

In the Reykjavik Study, among 9,681 women and 8,888 men without prior myocardial infarction followed up to 28 years, systolic blood pressure was a stronger risk factor for women, as was ECG-confirmed left ventricular hypertrophy (women HR 2.89, 95% CI 1.67-5.01; men HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.86-1.43).
Diabetes markers were also stronger in women: fasting blood glucose ≥6.7 mmol/L had HR 2.65 in women vs 2.08 in men, and self-reported diabetes similarly.

Smoking increased risk two- to five-fold in women, significantly higher than the doubling in men, while serum cholesterol was a significant risk factor in both sexes and triglyceride risk was significantly higher for women.

No—in this study, admission to a hospital with onsite coronary revascularization services was not associated with significantly better survival for elderly patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock.

Among 601 Medicare patients aged ≥65 with acute MI complicated by cardiogenic shock, 287 were admitted to hospitals without revascularization services and 314 to hospitals with coronary angioplasty and CABG facilities.

After adjustment for demographic, clinical, hospital, and treatment factors, onsite revascularization services were not associated with a significantly lower 30-day mortality (odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.47–1.45) or 1-year mortality (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.49–1.72).
No — this retrospective audit found postoperative antibiotics had no role in pain control, postoperative fever, secondary hemorrhage, or reduction in hospital stay.
Among 185 patients undergoing tonsillectomy with or without adenoidectomy (ages 2–53 years, mostly children), the audit reported no benefit of postoperative antibiotics for those morbidity outcomes.

However, because this is a single retrospective audit without a described control group or effect sizes, it suggests but does not definitively settle whether antibiotics decrease post-tonsillectomy morbidity.

Yes, further investigation is warranted after a convulsion with retinal haemorrhage, based on a prospective study of 153 children aged 2 months to 2 years seen in the emergency department after a convulsive episode.
In that study, one child had unilateral retinal haemorrhages following a simple febrile convulsion, and thorough investigation uncovered no other reason for the finding.
Because retinal haemorrhages are considered characteristic of child abuse, this rare occurrence (1 of 153) supports looking further to rule out systemic disorder or child abuse.

No, the evidence suggests pelvic CT is not routinely needed in renal cell carcinoma because in 400 RCC patients all pelvic abnormalities found on pelvic CT had already been detected by ultrasound or plain X-ray.
Only 14 (3.5%) had any pelvic CT abnormality and 6 (1.5%) had malignant findings (superficial bladder cancer, RCC in a pelvic kidney, or pelvic bone metastases), but none were new findings on CT.
The evidence is mixed: concentric leg muscle power was generally not related to running speed with changes of direction, while reactive strength showed some moderate significant correlations.

In 15 male participants experienced in sports involving sprints with changes of direction, 8 m sprints with various changes of direction were timed and compared with bilateral and unilateral leg extensor concentric power from an isokinetic squat and reactive strength from a drop jump.

Correlations between concentric leg power and change-of-direction speed were generally low and non-significant, whereas some moderate and significant (p<0.05) coefficients were found for reactive strength.
Yes—lower fasting plasma glucose (FPG) at diagnosis was associated with improved clinical and surrogate outcomes in the U.K.
Diabetes Prospective Study.

Among 5,088 of 5,102 participants, those with low FPG (<140 mg/dl) at diagnosis had fewer cases of retinopathy, abnormal biothesiometer measurements, and reported erectile dysfunction and a significantly reduced risk for each predefined clinical outcome except stroke, compared with higher FPG groups.

Both low and intermediate (140 to <180 mg/dl) FPG groups also had significantly reduced risk for progression of retinopathy, reduction in vibration sensory threshold, or development of microalbuminuria.

Yes—care by laparoscopic specialists was associated with improved treatment of acute cholecystitis, primarily a higher rate of successful laparoscopic cholecystectomy. In a retrospective review of 170 patients, 48 were cared for by three laparoscopic specialists (LS) and 122 by nine general surgeons (GS), with successful laparoscopic treatment in 65% of LS vs 36% of GS patients (p=0.001). Median postoperative hospital stay was shorter in the LS group (3 vs 5 days, p<0.01), while postoperative complications were similar (31% vs 37%, p=0.6). On logistic regression, LS group was a significant predictor of successful laparoscopic operation (p<0.01), but not of prolonged length of stay (p=0.21).
Yes—mossy fibers release GABA, based on monosynaptic GABAA receptor-mediated synaptic signals recorded in CA3 pyramidal neurons after recruiting dentate granule cells.

The evidence comes from hippocampal slices from 3- to 5-week-old guinea pigs, with whole-cell voltage clamp recordings from CA3 pyramidal cells and stimulating electrodes in stratum granulosum to recruit mossy fiber-CA3 projections.

These inhibitory signals satisfied mossy fiber-CA3 criteria (high sensitivity to metabotropic glutamate-receptor agonists, facilitation during repetitive stimulation, and NMDA receptor-independent long-term potentiation), and mossy fiber terminals also showed intense GABA and GAD67 immunoreactivity.
The passages report no sample sizes, comparison group, or numerical effect sizes for these findings.
The evidence is suggestive but does not establish that increased neutrophil migratory activity is a causal factor in ARDS.

In 17 adult blunt trauma patients (Injury Severity Score ≥18), neutrophils migrated significantly more to interleukin-8 (30 and 100 ng/mL) at admission and 8 and 24 hrs later than neutrophils from 9 normal volunteers (p<.05).
Neutrophil counts were also elevated at admission and declined over 24 hrs in patients who later developed ARDS.
However, this was a prospective observational study, and the authors only hypothesized that enhanced migration may be crucial in ARDS etiology, so it does not prove causation.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether HELLP syndrome is a manifestation of a systemic inflammatory response in pre-eclampsia.
The supplied passages describe a transversal study of 2,878 patients with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, of whom 1.15% (n=33) had HELLP syndrome.

They report maternal mortality of 0.4 per 10,000 live births, perinatal mortality of 1.62 per 10,000, renal damage in 84.5%, and correlations of pregnancy number with platelet count and creatinine clearance.
No inflammatory markers or comparisons relevant to a systemic inflammatory response are reported.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that withdrawal-induced anxiety in alcoholism is based on beta-endorphin deficiency, because the cited study shows only an association between lower beta-endorphin levels and greater anxiety during withdrawal.

In 60 alcoholics assessed on day 1 and day 14 after onset of withdrawal and 30 healthy volunteers, beta-endorphin was significantly lowered on both days relative to controls, and self-rated anxiety decreased significantly between day 1 and day 14.

Beta-endorphin levels were inversely correlated with anxiety on day 1 (r=-0.58) and day 14 (r=-0.71), and partial correlations controlling for ACTH indicated this relationship was largely independent of ACTH.
However, the passages do not establish that beta-endorphin deficiency causes withdrawal-induced anxiety, only that the two are correlated.
Yes, anorectal endosonography appears valuable in dyschesia because it demonstrated anal sphincter and m. puborectalis dysfunction during straining in patients compared with healthy controls.

In a prospective study, 20 consecutive patients with dyschesia and 20 healthy controls underwent linear anorectal endosonography with measurements at rest and during voluntary squeezing and straining.
The anal sphincter became paradoxically shorter and/or thicker during straining in 85% of patients versus 35% of controls, with significantly different changes in length (p<0.01).
The m. puborectalis showed paradoxical shortening and/or thickening in 80% of patients versus 30% of controls, with significant differences in both length and thickness (p<0.01).

No, routine circumcision in childhood is not supported by this study, since only 11 of 400 boys (2.7%) were considered in need of circumcision for specific indications such as prepucial orifice stenosis, a constrictive ring, repetitive balanopostitis, or xerosol balanitis.

In the same study, prepuce retractibility increased with age: non-retractile prepuce was 71.5% in boys under 1 year but only 1.6% in adolescents, while completely retractile prepuce rose from 5.5% to 82.3%.
Forced dilation during childhood was also not durable, as 106 boys had balano-prepucial adhesions again at later examination.
Thus, the passages support circumcision only for the minority with specific medical indications, not as a routine childhood procedure.

The evidence is mixed: prepuncture ultrasound did not improve internal jugular vein cannulation overall, but it did facilitate cannulation in patients in whom respiratory jugular venodilation was not identified.

In a randomized study of 240 adults undergoing general anesthesia for right internal jugular vein cannulation, when respiratory jugular venodilation was identified (188 patients, 78.3%), first-attempt success was 83.5% with landmarks versus 85.7% with ultrasound, success within 3 attempts was 96.9% versus 95.6%, and arterial puncture was 1.0% versus 3.3%.

In the 52 patients without identified respiratory jugular venodilation, ultrasound significantly improved first-attempt access (86.2% vs 30.4%, p<0.001) and success within 3 attempts (100% vs 78.3%, p<0.05), with arterial puncture 0% vs 13.0% for landmarks.
Yes—in high-risk metastatic breast cancer, first-line single-agent mitoxantrone was as effective as FEC combination chemotherapy on efficacy endpoints.

In a randomized trial of 260 previously untreated women with measurable high-risk metastatic breast cancer, mitoxantrone 12 mg/m2 was compared with fluorouracil, epirubicin, and cyclophosphamide (FEC) every 3 weeks.

Single-agent mitoxantrone did not differ significantly from FEC in response, objective remission rate, remission duration, time to response, time to best response, time to progression, or overall survival.
There was a significant difference in gain from treatment using a modified Brunner's score favoring single-agent treatment, and no evidence that any subgroup fared better with combination treatment.
Yes; ibuprofen increased perioperative blood loss during hip arthroplasty in a randomized double-blind trial.
In 50 patients scheduled for total hip replacement who were pretreated for 2 weeks, perioperative blood loss was 45% greater in the ibuprofen group than in the placebo group.
Total blood loss was 1161 ± 472 mL with ibuprofen versus 796 ± 337 mL with placebo.
Yes—a written information sheet improved recall: patients given written information scored significantly higher (48% correct answers) than those given verbal information alone (38% correct answers).

This was a prospective randomised controlled study in a specialist orthopaedic unit of 126 patients undergoing revision or primary total hip arthroplasty, with 65 patients receiving verbal information and 61 receiving written information.
Recall was tested with a questionnaire completed on admission, a mean of 18 days later.

The evidence is mixed for long-term survival and insufficient for morbidity: in gastric cancer patients after gastrectomy, BMI was associated with survival, but the direction differed by stage, and no morbidity comparison is reported.

In a retrospective comparison of patients with BMI<0.185 versus BMI>0.210 after gastrectomy with D2-lymphadenectomy, the lower-BMI group had significantly longer mean survival in stage 2 (1667 vs 1322 days, P=0.0240).
In contrast, the higher-BMI group had significantly longer mean survival in stage 3a (1431 vs 943 days, P=0.0071).
The study aimed to clarify BMI and long-term survival and compared morbidity and survival between these groups, but the supplied results do not report morbidity outcomes.

The evidence is mixed: in a VA cohort of 11,661 patients discharged with CHF, cardiology-only outpatient follow-up was not significantly associated with better 1-year survival than mixed general medicine plus cardiology care (adjusted risk ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.94-1.34). The lowest unadjusted mortality was in the mixed group (19%), while general medicine-only and no general medicine/cardiology follow-up had higher adjusted death risks (1.26, 95% CI 1.15-1.38 and 1.48, 95% CI 1.28-1.72, respectively) compared with mixed care. A second VA cohort showed consistent results, with significantly worse survival for general medicine-only versus mixed care (1.25, 95% CI 1.14-1.37). Thus, the passages support an association between combined general medicine and cardiology care and better survival, but they do not show that specialty care alone improves survival.

Yes, the evidence suggests some environmental and occupational factors are important in primary systemic vasculitis, based on a case-control study of 75 PSV cases and 273 controls (220 nonvasculitis, 19 secondary vasculitis, and 34 asthma controls).
Farming in the index year was associated with PSV (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.2-4.6), and high occupational silica exposure in the index year was associated with PSV (OR 3.0, 95% CI 1.0-8.4).

High occupational solvent exposure during the working lifetime was associated with PSV (OR 2.7, 95% CI 1.1-6.6), and drug allergy (OR 3.6, 95% CI 1.8-7.0) and allergy overall (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.2-3.9) were also associated with PSV.
No other significant associations were found, so the study supports importance for selected exposures rather than all environmental factors.
Yes, spinal subdural hematoma can be a sequela of a ruptured intracranial aneurysm, based on a single case report.

In that report, a 52-year-old woman with a ruptured internal carotid aneurysm and subarachnoid hemorrhage predominantly in the posterior fossa developed severe lower back and buttock pain on postoperative day 6, and MRI showed a lumbosacral subdural hematoma.
The hematoma was treated conservatively, diminished completely by 15 weeks, and she was discharged without neurologic deficit.
However, the passage notes such a case had never been reported before, so the evidence is limited to this single observation.
No—tumor depth did not have a major independent prognostic effect in soft tissue sarcoma once grade and tumor size were accounted for.
In a population-based series of 490 adults with extremity or trunk-wall soft tissue sarcoma, multivariate analysis showed no major prognostic effect of depth when grade and size were included.

Depth did affect prognosis in the subset of high-grade, large tumors, where deep-seated tumors had poorer survival, but this was explained by their larger mean size—large deep tumors averaged one third larger than large superficial tumors.

The evidence is mixed and comes from a decision-analysis model, not a clinical trial: it generally favors withholding anticoagulation after ICH, though anticoagulation may be preferred in selected deep hemispheric ICH patients with very high thromboembolic risk.

In a base case of a 69-year-old man with prior ICH and newly diagnosed nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, withholding anticoagulation improved quality-adjusted life expectancy by 1.9 QALYs for prior lobar ICH and by 0.3 QALYs for prior deep hemispheric ICH compared with warfarin.
Sensitivity analyses for deep ICH found anticoagulation could be preferred if the risk of thromboembolic stroke is particularly high.

The evidence is mixed/insufficient: in resected mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS) tissue, apoptotic markers were present but definitive apoptotic DNA fragmentation and nuclear morphology were not found.

In 15 drug-resistant epilepsy patients with MTS (6 women, 9 men; mean age 29 +/- 8 years), Bax immunopositivity was increased in almost all neurons and fractin, a caspase activity indicator, was detected in approximately 10% of neurons.
However, TUNEL staining showed no DNA fragmentation, and Hoechst-33258 or hematoxylin counterstaining showed no typical apoptotic nuclear changes.
Thus, these passages do not confirm that cell death in MTS is apoptotic, despite some apoptotic pathway activation.
Evidence is mixed: socioeconomic status was associated with worse quality of life in newly diagnosed lung cancer patients at baseline, but not at the three-month follow-up.

In a study of 129 patients, with complete baseline and follow-up data for 82, 57% were of lower socioeconomic status and had more health problems, less functioning, and more symptoms than affluent patients.
At baseline, significant differences were seen for physical mobility (P = 0.05), energy (P = 0.01), role functioning (P = 0.04), physical functioning (P = 0.03), and breathlessness (P = 0.02).
At follow-up, there was no significant difference between patient groups and no consistent pattern emerged.
Yes, a 9-month regimen appears sufficient in this small randomized trial, with complete response in all patients and no recurrence during follow-up.
In 40 patients with tuberculous enterocolitis, 22 were randomized to 9 months and 18 to 15 months of anti-tuberculous therapy.
Complete response was obtained in all patients in both groups, and no recurrence of active intestinal tuberculosis occurred during follow-up in either group.
Two patients in the 9-month group and one in the 15-month group required surgery for intestinal obstruction and perianal fistula, respectively.
However, the background notes that the duration of therapy had not been clarified in intestinal tuberculosis, and this was a small study.
Yes—in CD Fischer rats, Nd:YAG laser-induced thermo therapy (LITT) produced locoregional blood-brain barrier (BBB) opening and HPLC proved paclitaxel passage across the disrupted BBB.
The study used CD Fischer rats subjected to LITT of the left forebrain, with BBB disruption analyzed by Evans blue and immunohistochemistry and paclitaxel measured in brain and plasma by HPLC.
LITT induced locoregional extravasation of Evans blue, C3C, fibrinogen, and IgM, confirming BBB opening.
However, the passages do not provide glioma treatment outcomes or survival data, so they support a delivery concept but not yet proof of adjuvant glioma therapy efficacy.

The evidence is insufficient to answer whether early discharge with nurse home visits affects adequacy of newborn metabolic screening, because the only supplied study compares early discharge with traditional stay and does not mention nurse home visits.

In that study, among 3860 infants (1324 early discharge, 2536 traditional stay), early discharge infants had a higher rate of initial inadequate filter paper specimens (22.9% vs 14.3%, P<.0001) but a higher rate of repeat specimens after an inadequate initial specimen (85.0% vs 75.3%, P=.002).
Early discharge infants were also more likely to have an adequate specimen within the first 9 days of life (98.8% vs 96.7%, P=.0005).
Thus, the passages show effects of early discharge alone, not of nurse home visits, on screening adequacy.
Yes, a 2-day course was followed by increased self-assessed communication security and reported behavior changes in communicating with terminally ill patients.

The first three courses included 31 participants who rated their security in seven communication settings before, immediately after, and 3 months after the course, with important increases for communicating cancer diagnosis, recurrence, or advanced disease without curative approach.
Three months later, participants described multiple changes indicating increased sensitivity and professionalism in communication behavior.
These findings are based on self-assessment and course evaluation, so they support that communication can be taught but do not provide objective or controlled proof of skill acquisition.

The evidence is mixed: independent double reading of barium enemas increased positive results from 249 to 315 and potentially altered clinical treatment in 98 of 994 patients (9.9%), but it did not improve sensitivity for all lesions, which was 76.3% for both first and combined readings.
Specificity fell from 91.0% for the first reading to 86.4% for the combined reading, and agreement fell from a kappa value of 61.8 to 52.9.
The second reading added an average of 3.3 min, while sensitivity for adenocarcinomas was 100%.
Thus, the study shows trade-offs rather than a clear answer on whether double reading is necessary.

The evidence is insufficient to say whether a practicing surgeon can reliably detect early lymphedema; the supplied passages evaluate circumference-based detection in 90 breast cancer patients against an academic trial standard, not surgeon examination.
In that cohort, 39 lymphedema cases were identified, and sensitivity was 37% for a 10% circumference increase at two sites, 49% for a 10% increase at any site, and 91% for a 5% increase at any site.
The evidence is insufficient to say progression of valvar aortic stenosis can be predicted accurately, because the study identifies predictors but does not report an accuracy metric.

In 169 men and 88 women with aortic stenosis, aged 55.2 +/- 15.7 years at first and 63.4 +/- 15.6 years at second cardiac catheterization, progression rate depended on valvar calcification score and was exponentially correlated with initial aortic valve area, while age, sex, and etiology did not significantly influence progression.
The study reported that if AVA falls below 0.75 cm2 with VC=0, 0.8 with VC I, 0.9 with VC II, or 1.0 with VC III, aortic stenosis is probable to require surgery in the following years.
No—sub-classification of low-grade cerebellar astrocytoma was not clinically meaningful for prognosis in this cohort.

Among children aged 0-14 years treated in Denmark for cerebellar astrocytoma during 1960-1984 and followed until January 2001 or death, overall survival was 81% after 15-40 years, and no difference in survival time was demonstrated between pilocytic and fibrillary astrocytoma.
The Kernohan and WHO classification systems had no predictive value, and the Daumas-Duport system was unsuitable as a prognostic tool for low-grade posterior fossa astrocytomas.
No, the sequence of clamp application during open AAA surgery did not influence distal embolisation in the available randomized evidence.

In 40 patients undergoing AAA repair randomized to first clamping the proximal aorta or the iliac vessels, there was no difference between groups in the number of emboli passing through the superficial femoral arteries detected by transcranial Doppler (p=0.49).
The study also found no significant correlation between embolus number and dissection time, although current smokers had a significantly higher number of emboli (p=0.034).
These passages show no effect of clamp sequence on distal embolisation, but they are limited to one small trial.

Evidence is mixed or limited: among women with recurrent breast cancer, unadjusted survival improved significantly across five recurrence-year cohorts from 1974 to 2000 (P<0.001), but after adjustment for prognostic factors the improvement was only a trend, with a 1% reduction in risk for each increasing year.
This rests on 834 women who developed recurrent breast cancer between November 1974 and December 2000 after prior adjuvant anthracycline-based treatment, divided by year of recurrence.
The passages address only recurrent breast cancer, so they do not settle whether breast cancer survival overall is improving.
Yes, pain appears to be a clinically relevant problem in general adult psychiatry, based on its high prevalence and associated impairment and unfitness for work.

In a cross-sectional questionnaire study of 106 patients primarily diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder in general adult psychiatry, the point prevalence of pain was about 50%, the 6-month prevalence was 75.5%, and the 12-month prevalence was 76.5%.
The most frequent complaints were low back pain, headache, and shoulder and neck pain.
Almost 10% of all patients reported pain continuing at least 3 months in the past year, and impairment and unfitness for work were related to specific psychiatric diagnosis.
Statistically significant risk factors for pain were depression (OR=6.05) and the number of past admissions to psychiatric hospitals (OR=3.609).
Yes, the evidence suggests a favorable subset: among prostate cancer patients who developed metastases, those with ≤5 metastatic lesions had better outcomes than those with >5 lesions.
In a retrospective analysis of 369 patients with Stage T1-T3aN0-NXM0 prostate cancer treated with external beam radiotherapy, 74 (20%) developed metastases.
Patients with ≤5 metastatic lesions had superior overall survival (73% at 5 years and 36% at 10 years) compared with those with >5 lesions (45% and 18%; p=0.02).
Metastasis-free survival and time from diagnosis to bone metastasis were also superior for the ≤5 lesion group, although survival after bone metastasis diagnosis did not differ significantly.
Yes, CT can help predict the level of CSF block in tuberculous hydrocephalus, but only via the shape of the third ventricle.

In 50 children with communicating and 34 with non-communicating hydrocephalus classified by air-encephalography, the only CT finding that correlated with the type of hydrocephalus was third ventricle shape.
Significantly more children with non-communicating hydrocephalus had a rounded third ventricle than those with communicating hydrocephalus.
Yes—radiotherapy around the time of pregnancy appears to increase the risk of breast cancer in women treated for Hodgkin's disease.
The evidence comes from 382 women treated with radiotherapy for Hodgkin's disease, comparing those who received radiotherapy around pregnancy with those who were not pregnant.
Overall breast cancer incidence was 16.0% vs 2.3% (p=0.0001), and 10- and 15-year actuarial rates were 6.7% and 32.6% vs 0.4% and 1.7%, respectively.

In multivariate analysis, pregnancy around radiotherapy was the only variable associated with increased breast cancer risk, and radiotherapy during pregnancy or within 1 month of pregnancy had a hazard ratio of 22.49 (95% CI 5.56-90.88, p<0.001) compared with nonpregnant women and those irradiated later than 1 month after pregnancy.
Yes, fear of anaphylaxis—together with fear of dissemination—appears to discourage wider adoption of percutaneous and laparoscopic treatment for liver hydatid cysts.
In a survey of 30 surgeons in northern Jordan, only 3 (10%) considered laparoscopy as first-line treatment.
Among the 27 surgeons who did not consider percutaneous or laparoscopic treatment, 21 (78%) gave fear of anaphylaxis and/or dissemination as the main reason for not using minimal-access techniques.
The passages support anaphylaxis fear as part of the main reported barrier, though they combine it with dissemination rather than isolating anaphylactic shock alone.
No, higher rates of depression in women are not accounted for by differential symptom reporting in this study.

In a population-based 13-year follow-up of 1,727 community-dwelling adults in East Baltimore, women and men did not significantly differ in self-reported depression symptoms across the nine symptom groups for major depression after adjustment for age, ethnicity, education, marital status, and employment.
For example, the adjusted direct effect of gender on report of sadness was 0.105 (95% CI -0.113 to 0.323), not significantly different from the null.
Thus, the evidence indicates that differential symptom reporting does not explain the higher depression rates in women.

The evidence is mixed: patients with diabetes receive similar messages from dietitians and nurses on typical carbohydrate recommendations but different messages on fiber, glycemic index, and hypoglycemia treatment.

In a survey of 366 certified diabetes educators (207 RNs and 159 RDs) in the southern United States, no statistically significant differences were found between RNs and RDs in typical carbohydrate recommendations for diabetes treatment.

However, RDs were more likely than RNs to recommend fiber intake or use of the glycemic index, and RNs were more likely than RDs to recommend consuming a carbohydrate source with protein to treat hypoglycemia.
The passages do not directly address profiling quality of care or peer review, so the evidence is insufficient to settle whether peer review has a role.
They report a reliability study of a structured implicit chart review instrument using 12 reviewers and 496 reviews of 70 patient records from 26 VA sites.

Reliability of a single physician review was low for COPD and acute conditions (intra-class correlation 0.16–0.26) but significantly higher for diabetes and hypertension (0.46), driven by reviewers distinguishing more differences between patients rather than less noise.
Thus, physician review reliability varies by condition, but the passages do not evaluate its use for profiling.
No, acute changes in heart rate by isoproterenol did not meaningfully affect aortic stiffness in patients with hypertension.

In 17 hypertensive patients (mean age 59 +/- 9 years), isoproterenol was used to increase heart rate gradually while aortic stiffness was assessed by carotid-to-femoral pulse wave velocity, compliance, and compliance index.

There were no significant differences among heart-rate change groups for deltaPWV, deltaC, or deltaCi (p>0.05 each), and deltaHR did not significantly correlate with deltaPWV or deltaC (r=0.18 and 0.13, respectively; p>0.05 each). deltaCi showed only a poor correlation with deltaHR (r=0.22, p<0.05) that explained 4.6% of its variance, supporting no meaningful effect of acute isoproterenol-induced heart rate changes on aortic stiffness.

Yes—the supplied paper proposes the Omega-3 Index as a new risk factor for death from coronary heart disease, resting on the finding that the RBC EPA+DHA index was inversely associated with CHD mortality.
In several published primary and secondary prevention studies, an Omega-3 Index ≥8% was associated with the greatest cardioprotection and ≤4% with the least.

The rationale includes that low EPA+DHA intake or blood levels are independently associated with increased CHD death risk, and fish or fish oil reduced total and CHD mortality at about 1 g/day in randomized secondary prevention trials.
These passages support the proposal but describe it as a putative marker being validated rather than definitively established.
Yes—partial remission after a major depressive episode was an important risk factor for relapse over a 4-year follow-up.

In 139 Spanish outpatients with DSM-III-R unipolar major depressive episode followed monthly for more than 4 years, the relapse rate was higher in partial remission (91.4%) than in complete remission (51.3%).
Partial remission versus complete remission was one of four predictive relapse factors and was reported as the most powerful predictive factor.
Limitations included decreasing sample size during follow-up and difficulty warranting treatment compliance.
Yes, the evidence supports c-Kit-dependent growth as a potential therapeutic target in uveal melanoma.

In 134 paraffin-embedded uveal melanomas and eight fresh-frozen samples, c-kit was expressed in 84/134 and 6/8, respectively, and cultured uveal melanoma cell lines showed strong c-kit expression and tyrosine phosphorylation compared with cutaneous melanoma cells.

The three uveal melanoma cell lines also expressed c-kit ligand, suggesting autocrine/paracrine stimulation, and treatment with STI571 blocked c-kit autophosphorylation and caused cell death with an IC50 below 2.5 microM for both phosphorylation and proliferation.

The evidence suggests limited relevance and applicability of sports medicine journals to practitioners and athletes, because an analysis of original research, short reports, and case reports in four major sport and exercise medicine journals found that the most common topic was sports science and very few studies related to treatment of injuries and medical conditions.
The same analysis found that the majority of published articles used healthy subjects sampled from the sedentary population, with few studies carried out on injured participants.
These findings indicate limited direct applicability to everyday clinical practice and injured athletes, although the passages do not provide exact counts or a definitive overall judgment.
The evidence is mixed: reduced arm spasticity was associated with improved arm function in some botulinum toxin dose groups but not others.

In a pooled analysis of individual data from stroke patients in two randomized controlled trials of intramuscular botulinum toxin, maximum change in spasticity and maximum change in arm function were related independent of treatment (rho = -0.2822, p = 0.0008, n = 137).

The relationship was clear for patients treated with botulinum toxin (Dysport) at 500 or 1000 units (rho = -0.5679, p = 0.0090, n = 22; rho = -0.4430, p = 0.0018, n = 47), but not for placebo or 1500 units.
Timing was also mixed: changes were concurrent in 47 patients, spasticity improvement preceded function in 26, and function improvement preceded spasticity in 18.

No, the evidence suggests there is no general early-adopter trait across drug groups, based on a Danish general practitioner cohort in which adoption of one drug group was poorly associated with adoption of others (r ≤ 0.49).

The study analyzed prescribing of angiotensin-II antagonists, triptans, selective cyclo-oxygenase-2 antagonists, and esomeprazol, using measures such as adoption time, cumulative incidence, preference proportion, incidence rate, and prescription cost/volume, and found that early adoption of one type of drug was not associated with early adoption of another.
Thus, while individual physicians may adopt a specific drug early, the passages do not support a consistent personal trait of being an early adopter across drug classes.
Yes—expert breast pathology assessment appears necessary for DCIS management because secondary review changed treatment recommendations in 43% of cases.
In 481 patients with DCIS referred to a single regional cancer centre between 1982 and 2000, pathology review was performed on 350 (73%).

From 1996 to 2000, secondary assessments changed local recurrence risk in 100 cases (29%) and treatment recommendation in 93 (43%) cases, although inter-observer agreement was high for main pathologic features.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that adding 2-methoxyestradiol (2ME) can reduce chemotherapeutic dosages in the treatment of human ovarian cancer, because the available data are only from in vitro cell-line experiments.

In two human ovarian cancer cell lines, 2ME (0.8–25 microM) combined with various chemotherapeutics produced a significant additive inhibitory effect on proliferation with epirubicine and carboplatin at the lower concentration range of those chemotherapeutics.
However, the passages do not report clinical treatment, dose-reduction endpoints, or whether lower chemotherapeutic doses achieved equivalent efficacy, so they do not directly settle the question.
Yes, prior benign prostate biopsy is associated with more favorable outcomes after radical perineal prostatectomy.

Among 1369 patients with clinically localized prostate cancer, 203 with at least one prior benign biopsy had more organ-confined disease (74% vs 64%, P<0.001), less margin-positive disease (9.8% vs 18%), and lower biochemical failure (12% vs 20%, P=0.01) than 1115 patients with no prior biopsy.
They also had improved biochemical disease-free survival and lower odds of biochemical failure (OR 0.57, P<0.001).
Yes—socioeconomic status matters for postpartum learning needs, specifically unmet learning needs.

In a survey of 1,250 postpartum women from 5 Ontario hospitals (890 interviewed 4 weeks after discharge; about 17% low socioeconomic status), women of low socioeconomic status were significantly more likely to report unmet learning needs related to 9 of 10 topics compared with women of higher socioeconomic status.
However, there were few differences in identified concerns: breastfeeding and signs of infant illness were the most frequent concerns regardless of socioeconomic status.
For most topics, significantly more women in both groups identified learning needs 4 weeks after discharge than had corresponding concerns while in hospital.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that inhaled steroids themselves differ from cromones in hospital admission rates, because the passages report only an ecological comparison between two provinces with different overall asthma medication profiles.

In children under 16 years with asthma from 1995-1999, Kuopio had 23% on cromones, 51% on inhaled steroids, and 26% on cromones plus intermittent steroids, whereas Oulu had 5%, 93%, and 2%, respectively.

In children aged ≥6 years, Oulu had lower average annual total admissions (0.3/1000 vs 1.2/1000, p<0.001), first admissions (0.2/1000 vs 1.0/1000, p<0.001), readmissions (6.3% vs 19.3%, p<0.05), and hospital days (0.7/1000 vs 3.8/1000, p<0.001), with similar but less prominent differences in children 2-5 years.

These data associate a province with much greater inhaled steroid use and less cromone use with lower admission rates, but they do not directly compare children treated with inhaled steroids versus cromones, so they cannot establish a difference between the two drug classes.

No, this study found that higher private referral rates did not reduce NHS demand; instead, NHS referral rates were higher in wards with the highest private referral rates. Among 17,137 GP referrals from 10 UK practices in 2001, 90.4% were to the NHS and 9.6% to the private sector. After adjustment for deprivation and practice, the NHS referral rate was significantly higher in wards in the top fifth for private referral rates than in the bottom fifth (rate ratio 1.40, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.71, p=0.001). This is an observational comparison, so it shows an association rather than proving that increased private use causes NHS demand to fall.
No—the available retrospective evidence found no benefit from adjuvant radiation in stage III thymoma.
In 45 patients with stage III disease (36 complete resections), adding adjuvant radiotherapy did not alter local or distant recurrence rates.
Ten-year disease-specific survival was 75% without radiation versus 79% with radiation (p = 0.21), with similar baseline prognostic factors.
This single small retrospective series therefore does not support routine adjuvant radiation, but it cannot by itself definitively settle the question.

Bottom line: Yes, serum pancreatic lipase appears to be a better biomarker than serum amylase for acute pancreatitis, so the evidence supports replacing amylase with lipase. In 10,931 patients with 17,531 enzyme measurements, receiver operating characteristic analysis of initial Emergency Department samples showed improved diagnostic accuracy for serum pancreatic lipase (AUC 0.948) versus serum amylase (AUC 0.906, P<0.05). At diagnostic thresholds, lipase had sensitivity 90.3% and specificity 93%, compared with amylase sensitivity 76.8% and specificity 92.6%. Among acute pancreatitis patients, 18.8% lacked elevated serum amylase on the first emergency department measurement versus only 2.9% lacking elevated serum pancreatic lipase.
Yes, some U.S. states appear to have higher or lower injury mortality rates than others.
In a study of 12 states from 1983 to 1995, the six states with the highest road traffic death rates were compared with the six states with the lowest rates across 13 injury categories.
Among the high-road-traffic-death states, 74% also had above-average rates for other injuries, while 85% of the low-road-traffic-death states had below-average rates for other injuries.
This supports the hypothesis that injury mortality patterns cluster by state, though the evidence is limited to these 12 states and the specified period.
Yes, grandmultiparity appears to be an independent risk factor for adverse perinatal outcomes after adjustment for potential confounders.

In a California study of 25,512 grandmultiparous women with singleton deliveries versus 265,060 multiparous women aged 30 years or older, grandmultiparous women had significantly higher adjusted risks of abruptio placentae (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.2–1.5), preterm delivery (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.2–1.4), fetal macrosomia (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.4–1.6), neonatal death (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3–1.8), postpartum hemorrhage (OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.1–1.3), and blood transfusion (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.3–1.8).

Yes, the supplied evidence links fast food consumption to increased asthma symptoms, though it is cross-sectional and cannot prove causation. In 1321 children (mean age 11.4) in Hastings, New Zealand, hamburger consumption was independently associated with a history of wheeze (less than once/week OR=1.44, 95% CI 1.06-1.96; 1+ times/week OR=1.65, 95% CI 1.07-2.52) and current wheeze (1+ times/week OR=1.81, 95% CI 1.10-2.98). Takeaway consumption 1+ times/week was marginally significantly related to exercise-induced bronchial hyperresponsiveness (OR=2.41, 95% CI 0.99-5.91), but there was no effect on atopy.
Yes, a prospective observational study supports a potential role for uterine natural killer (uNK) cells in irregular endometrial bleeding in menopausal hormone therapy (HT) users.

Among 117 postmenopausal women taking combined HT, endometrial CD56+ uNK cells were significantly increased in biopsies taken during bleeding episodes compared with HT users with no bleeding (P<0.001), and the highest IL-15 expression was also seen during bleeding.
No clear relationship between killer Ig like receptor genotype and bleeding on HT was observed.
These findings suggest a potential role for uNK cells, but the observational design does not establish causality.
Yes, correlated results are possible from homebrew quantitative real-time PCR assays for BCRABL, based on a strong correlation found despite different laboratory methods.

In 70 clinical specimens, Vanderbilt and Virginia Commonwealth used different RNA isolation, cDNA synthesis, BCR control cell line, and PCR primer/probe sequences, yet 43 samples were negative at both sites and 22 BCRABL-positive paired results gave a Spearman r_s of 0.9435 (p<0.00001).
Only one discordant result occurred, for consecutive samples from a patient with low BCRABL copy number due to minimal RNA yield at one laboratory.

No, bedside assessment did not reliably exclude aspiration after acute stroke: among 94 consecutive patients admitted within 24 h of stroke who underwent videofluoroscopy, 20 (21%) were aspirating, but bedside assessment missed this in 10.

Speech and language therapist bedside assessment had a sensitivity of 47% and negative predictive value of 85% for aspiration, while a model using weak voluntary cough and altered conscious level had sensitivity 75% and NPV 91%.
Thus the passages show substantial false-negative rates and do not support using bedside assessment alone to reliably rule out aspiration.
No — in this study, AVPR1A microsatellites were not significantly related to hypersexuality in children with a prepubertal and early adolescent bipolar disorder phenotype.

Among 83 PEA-BP probands, transmission disequilibrium tests and case-control analyses found no significant associations between hypersexuality or uninhibited people-seeking and the number of AVPR1A GATA or complex repeats, using 32 complete trios for the GATA repeat and 34 for the complex repeat.

The study had about 80% power at p<0.05 to detect odds ratios of 5.0 and 4.0 in family-based analyses and 3.5 and 2.6 in case-control analyses for allele frequencies of 0.1 and 0.5, respectively, so it does not support a relationship, though it may not rule out smaller effects.

Small differences exist between Landolt C and Snellen E acuity in strabismus amblyopia, with Snellen E acuity slightly higher. In 39 patients with strabismus amblyopia, mean decimal acuity was 0.14 for Landolt C and 0.16 for Snellen E. The mean difference was 0.55 lines, with higher values for Snellen E, similar to the entire group of 100 patients with various eye disorders and 13 healthy volunteers.
Yes, end-tidal CO2 correlated with arterial CO2 in ventilated extremely low birth weight infants during the first week of life, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.81.
This rests on 754 paired EtCO2 and arterial CO2 measurements from 31 ELBW infants, where EtCO2 was usually lower than PaCO2 and only 89/754 (11.8%) pairs had EtCO2 higher.
The overall bias was 5.6 +/- 6.9 mmHg (95% CI 5.11-6.09), and EtCO2 ranges of 30 to 50 mmHg identified 84% of instances with PaCO2 between 35 and 55 mmHg.

The evidence is mixed or lesion-dependent: hydrophilic guidewires significantly improved technical success rates for some peripheral PTA lesions, specifically SFA stenosis and iliac and SFA occlusions, but not for iliac stenosis.
In 125 procedures, conventional guidewires were used first and hydrophilic guidewires if needed for iliac and SFA stenoses or occlusions.

Technical success rates with conventional vs hydrophilic wires were 96% vs 100% for iliac stenosis (no significant difference), 60% vs 96% for iliac occlusions, 84% vs 100% for femoral stenosis, 64% vs 96% for femoral occlusions <10 cm, and 48% vs 88% for femoral occlusions >10 cm.
Yes—among the cytokines measured in secretin-stimulated pancreatic juice, only interleukin-8 discriminated the presence of pancreatic disease from normal pancreas.

In 118 patients with abdominal pain compatible with pancreatic origin, multivariate analysis found interleukin-8 distinguished normal pancreas from chronic pancreatitis (P =.011), pancreatic cancer (P =.044), and the presence of pancreatic diseases (P =.007).
However, individual cytokine concentrations did not significantly differ between chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer, so they did not distinguish those two disease types.
Yes, obstructive sleep apnea severity predicts the need for high continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).
In 353 consecutive OSA patients who had successful manual CPAP titration, high CPAP (≥12 cm H2O) was required in 2 (6.9%) with mild, 6 (5.8%) with moderate, and 63 (28.6%) with severe OSA.
On logistic regression, high CPAP use was 5.90 times more frequent in severe OSA patients after adjustment for other variables (95% CI 2.67-13.1).

No, the evidence suggests trainees are not consistently learning complete surgical care, because complete in-hospital continuity (preoperative and postoperative assessment) occurred in only 57% of cases, involvement in the decision to operate was 17%, and follow-up clinic assessment was 3%.
In a prospective cohort of 159 vascular procedures at two University of British Columbia teaching hospitals, preoperative assessment was 67% and postoperative ward assessment was 79%.

Emergent cases had higher preoperative assessment than elective cases (92% vs 63%, P<.05), and elective cases admitted before the day of surgery had higher preoperative assessment (78% vs 58%, P<.05) and decision-to-operate involvement (16% vs 4%, P<.05) than same-day admissions.
These findings show gaps in the full spectrum of care, but the study measured resident involvement rather than learning outcomes.
Yes, there was a difference: prefilled textured saline breast implants had higher cumulative deflation rates than standard textured saline implants over 4 years.

In a consecutive series of 500 Poly Implant Prosthesis prefilled textured saline implants compared with 500 Mentor Siltex textured saline implants, cumulative deflation rates were 1.2% vs 0.2% at year 1 (not significant), 5.6% vs 0.6% at year 2, 11.4% vs 1.6% at year 3, and 15.4% vs 4.4% at year 4.
The differences were statistically significant at years 2, 3, and 4 (p<0.001 for each), but not at year 1 (p>0.05).
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether histological features influence clinical presentation and outcome in pituitary apoplexy.

A retrospective analysis of 59 patients divided them into infarction alone (22 patients) and hemorrhagic infarction and/or frank hemorrhage (37 patients) and compared presenting symptoms, clinical features, endocrinological status, and outcome between the groups.
However, the supplied passages do not report the results of these comparisons, so they do not show whether any differences were found.

Yes—preoperative tracheobronchoscopy mattered in newborns with esophageal atresia, being clinically useful in 28 of 62 patients (45.2%) and crucial in modifying the surgical approach in 15 of 62 (24.2%).

In a 1997–2003 series of 62 newborns with EA, preoperative TBS found unsuspected proximal fistula in 3 of 9 type A patients (reclassified as type B), plus 2 H-type fistulas and 4 previously undetected respiratory tree malformations.
It also allowed Fogarty catheter occlusion of carinal fistulas in 14 type C patients to improve ventilation during repair, with no complications observed.
The study does not compare TBS with no TBS, so it shows diagnostic and surgical impact but not comparative outcome benefit.
No, fetal gender was not associated with emergency department visits for asthma during pregnancy.
In a study of 109,173 live singleton deliveries, 530 women had at least one ED visit for asthma during pregnancy, and fetal gender was included as a predictor in multivariable logistic regression.
The odds ratio for having an ED visit for asthma by fetal gender was 1.01 (95% CI 0.85–1.19), indicating no significant association.
Fetal gender also was not a significant predictor of adverse pregnancy outcomes among women who had an asthma ED visit during pregnancy.
The evidence is mixed: French lay people and psychologists found breaching confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from an STD much more acceptable than physicians did.
In a French study, 144 lay people, 10 psychologists, and 7 physicians rated acceptability across 48 scenarios.
Mean acceptability ratings were 11.76 for lay people, 9.28 for psychologists, and 2.90 for physicians on a 0–22 scale.

Among lay participants, cluster analysis found some who considered it always acceptable (n = 14), some depending on circumstances (n = 87), some requiring expert consultation (n = 30), and some never acceptable (n = 13).
The patient's stated intentions to protect and inform his wife had the greatest impact on acceptability.
The evidence suggests no—pneumologists' skepticism is not justified by this study, since cytostatic treatment was an independent predictor of better survival in advanced NSCLC.
In 190 patients with stage IV or IIIB NSCLC and ECOG ≤2, median survival was 31 weeks, and cytostatic treatment was associated with a hazard ratio of 1.85 (95% CI 1.25–2.76; P=.002).

Among ECOG 0–1 patients, treatment and weight loss were significant prognostic factors, while ECOG 2 patients had median survival of 15 weeks with cytostatic treatment versus 11 weeks with symptomatic treatment.
However, the study reports an association rather than randomized evidence, so it supports but does not definitively settle the question.
No—based on this comparison, decisional algorithms cannot replace global introspection for individual causality assessment of spontaneously reported ADRs.
In 500 adverse reports, 15 algorithms were compared with WHO global introspection, using 'possible' as the lower limit for drug-relatedness.
The algorithms had high sensitivity (average 93%, PPV 89%) but low specificity (average 7%, NPV 31%).
This low specificity means they poorly identified non-drug-related reports, so they would not be a reliable substitute for global introspection.

No, routine chest radiography after transbronchial biopsy appears not to be necessary, because in 350 consecutive patients undergoing flexible bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, routine CXR found pneumothorax in only 10 (2.9%) and most were symptomatic.

Seven patients had symptoms strongly suggestive of pneumothorax before CXR, including four with large (>10%) pneumothorax, while the three asymptomatic patients had only minimal (<=10%) pneumothorax that resolved completely 24 to 48 h later.
The evidence is mixed: uterine myomas do not uniformly grow during pregnancy; in 107 pregnant patients with myomas, many shrank while a substantial minority enlarged.
Between the first half of pregnancy and 20–30 weeks, 55.1% decreased in volume (mean decrease 35% ± 4%) and 44.9% enlarged (mean increase 69% ± 11%).
Between 20–30 weeks and 31 weeks to term, 75% became smaller (mean decrease 30% ± 3%) and 25% enlarged (mean increase 102% ± 62%).
These data come from 107 patients diagnosed with uterine myomas during pregnancy who had at least two obstetrical ultrasounds in different periods.
Yes—among 1,014 consecutive patients undergoing coronary angiography, complex coronary lesions were more frequent in those with diabetes mellitus.
