In diabetics (n=281) versus nondiabetics (n=733), bifurcation lesions occurred in 9.8% versus 4.3% (P=0.001) and ostial lesions in 38.4% versus 29.2% (P=0.003).
Diabetes was also an independent predictor of bifurcation lesions (OR=2.27, P=0.004) and ostial lesions (OR=1.40, P=0.027) in multivariate analysis.
Yes, a patient's self-reported health-related quality of life is a prognostic factor for survival in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, based on specific domains retained as independent predictors.

In 391 advanced NSCLC patients, pretreatment EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-LC13 scores were analyzed with Cox models, and multivariate analysis retained self-reported pain (HR 1.11, 95% CI 1.07-1.16, P<0.001) and dysphagia (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.04-1.21, P=0.003) as independent prognostic factors for survival.
A 10-point worse score in pain and dysphagia corresponded to an 11% and 12% increased likelihood of death, respectively.
No, supervised colorectal trainees did not differ significantly from consultants in the quality of TME surgery, based on mesorectal grading.

Among 130 consecutive patients undergoing potentially curative rectal cancer resection, 89 operations were by consultants and 41 by supervised senior colorectal trainees; good mesorectum was found in 49% versus 41.5%, with no statistically significant difference (P = 0.717).
Local recurrence was also similar, 7.8% for consultants versus 9.5% for trainees (P = 0.719).
No—in a retrospective series of 236 patients with multinodular goiter undergoing thyroidectomy, frozen section did not alter intraoperative management in any of the 135 patients who had it.
Among those 135, 4 (3%) were later diagnosed with thyroid cancer on permanent histology and 3 frozen sections were misread as benign, for a sensitivity of only 25%.
The study compared patients who had frozen section with those who did not and found no differences in age, gender, or incidence of malignancy.
No, first-trimester folic acid use did not protect against congenital heart defects among Down syndrome children in this study.

The analysis included women with liveborn Down syndrome children from the Slone Epidemiology Center Birth Defects Study (1976-1997), comparing 223 Down syndrome children with heart anomalies to 184 Down syndrome children without heart anomalies.
Exposure was any folic acid-containing product used at least 4 days per week during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
Of cases, 49% were exposed versus 46% of controls, with adjusted OR 0.95 (95% CI 0.61-1.47) and no protective effect found for conotruncal defects, VSDs, ASDs, or ECDs.

No, the available evidence suggests endoaortic balloon occlusion is not safe for surgical management of the atherosclerotic ascending aorta, as it was independently associated with in-hospital death (odds ratio 5.609, 95% CI 2.684–11.719).
In a series of 2,172 consecutive patients, endoaortic occlusion was used in 52 patients selected by preoperative aortic calcifications or intraoperative epiaortic ultrasonography.
In-hospital death occurred in 25% of the endoaortic occlusion group versus 4.2% of all other patients (p<0.0001) and exceeded the expected 10.5% by EUROSCORE (p=0.05).
The balloon had to be replaced by conventional cross-clamping in 19.2% due to incomplete occlusion, hindered exposure, or balloon rupture, and stroke occurred in 3.8% versus 0.8% (p=0.067).
Yes—obstructive sleep apnea appears to affect aerobic fitness, though the direction differs by severity.
In a retrospective cohort of 247 patients with OSA, VO2max from cycle ergometry was compared with normative data from 1.4 million US Air Force tests.

Overall, individuals with OSA had increased VO2max versus the normalized US Air Force data (p<.001), but patients with an apnea-hypopnea index greater than 20 had decreased VO2max compared with normalized values (p<.001).
No differences in VO2max were observed after medical or surgical therapy for OSA.
The evidence is mixed: overall long-term scores were similar between transanal endorectal pull-through (TERPT) and conventional transabdominal (ABD) pull-through, but specific domains differed.

In a review of 41 patients over 3 years old with Hirschsprung disease (TERPT n = 20; ABD n = 21), families were interviewed and scored with a 15-item post-pull-through long-term outcome questionnaire.
Continence score was significantly better in the ABD group, while stool pattern score was better in the TERPT group.
After controlling for age, age did not significantly affect the long-term scoring outcome between groups.

No, fluoroscopy is not essential for retrieval of lower ureteric stones in most patients; in a prospective series of 110 patients with lower ureteral calculi (mean stone size 8.7 mm) who underwent ureteroscopic removal without fluoroscopy, complete clearance was achieved without fluoroscopy in 99 patients (94.2%).
Fluoroscopy was required in only 6 patients (4%) for indications such as calcified stricture, duplex system, a narrow and tortuous meatus, or confirmation of spontaneous stone passage.
Even among 13 patients who needed balloon dilatation, this was successfully done without fluoroscopy.
Thus the evidence indicates fluoroscopy is not routinely essential, though it may be needed in selected cases.

No, the supplied evidence does not demonstrate a need for neck dissection in patients with metastatic carcinoma to cervical nodes from an unknown head and neck primary. In a study of 61 such patients treated curatively with radiotherapy, 20 underwent neck dissection and 41 had biopsy only. There was no statistically significant difference in 8-year overall survival (64.8% vs 67.6%, p =.64) or local relapse-free survival (75% vs 74.5%, p =.57) between the neck dissection and biopsy groups. However, this single study does not definitively settle the question, as it does not report other outcomes or complications.
Yes, the evidence supports a stretch-sensitive KCNQ1 mutation linking genetic and environmental factors in AF pathogenesis, based on the R14C mutation identified in one family with AF.

In 50 families with AF screened for KCNQ1, KCNE1, KCNE2, and KCNE3 mutations, one missense KCNQ1 mutation (R14C) was found in a family with high hypertension prevalence, and AF occurred only in older genotype-positive individuals who had developed atrial dilation.

When wild-type or R14C KCNQ1 was expressed with KCNE1 in CHO cells, patch-clamp studies showed no significant differences at baseline or after forskolin, but after hypotonic solution to elicit cell swelling/stretch, mutant channels showed a marked current increase, leftward shift in activation voltage dependence, altered kinetics, and shortened modeled atrial action potential duration.
Yes—size-reducing ascending aortoplasty with external reinforcement can be an option in selected patients, though the supplied evidence notes that indications are not established.

In a retrospective study of 531 patients with ascending aortic aneurysm or ectasia (45–76 mm), 50 underwent size-reducing aortoplasty with a non-coated Dacron external reinforcement, often combined with aortic valve replacement, subvalvular myectomy, or CABG.

The procedure had 2% hospital mortality, reduced CT diameters from 55.8±9 mm to 40.5±6.2 mm and echocardiographic diameters from 54.1±6.7 mm to 38.7±7.1 mm (p<0.002), with stable results at a mean 70-month follow-up.
Evidence is mixed: bile duct sludge differed from common bile duct stones in frequency and some associations, but not in recurrence after endoscopic clearance.

In 228 patients undergoing ERCP for suspected choledocholithiasis, sludge without stones occurred in 14% (31/228), was more common in females, and was less often associated with CBD dilation than stones.
After endoscopic clearance, recurrent CBD stones occurred in 16% (5/31) of sludge patients versus 17% (33/197) of stone patients (p = 0.99), and other risk factors did not differ statistically.
Yes—better ambulatory process of care predicted less decline in health-related quality of life among patients with chronic disease.

In a prospective cohort of 963 managed-care patients with chronic disease from three west coast states, better process scores were associated with smaller declines in SF-12 physical component scores over 30 months after adjustment for burden of illness (p=.014).
Applying the best quartile of process of care to patients currently receiving poor process was associated with a 4.24-point increment in change in SF-12 physical component summary scores.
Yes, renal warm ischemia over 30 minutes during laparoscopic partial nephrectomy was possible in the reported cases.

In a study of 18 patients who underwent laparoscopic partial nephrectomy with warm ischemia time >30 min, kidney damage and renal function markers showed complete return to the normal range at 1 year with no statistical difference across time points.
Glomerular filtration rate was not significantly different before and 3 months after surgery.
Scintigraphy of the operated kidney decreased from 48.35% before surgery to 36.88% on postoperative day 5, then recovered to 40.56% at 3 months and 42.8% at 1 year.
Yes, shaving the incision site before spinal surgery increased the postoperative infection rate in a prospective randomized clinical study.
In 789 patients scheduled for spinal surgery, 371 had the site shaved immediately before surgery and 418 did not.
Postoperative infection developed in 4 shaved patients versus 1 unshaved patient (P<0.01).

Yes—breast cancer prognosis appears to be inherited, based on a Swedish population-based cohort showing that relatives of women with poor prognosis had worse survival. In 2,787 mother-daughter and 831 sister pairs with breast cancer diagnosed from 1961 to 2001, 5-year survival was 87% among daughters whose mothers died within 5 years versus 91% if the mother was alive (p=0.03), and 70% versus 88% among sisters (p=0.001). After adjustment, daughters and sisters of a proband with poor prognosis had 60% higher 5-year breast cancer mortality than those of a proband with good prognosis (HR 1.6, 95% CI 1.2–2.2; p for trend 0.002), with a slightly stronger association among sisters (HR 1.8) than daughters (HR 1.6).

The evidence is mixed: a 30-second antismoking trailer-style advertisement before a movie significantly increased non-smokers' belief that smoking in the movie was not OK (47.8% vs 43.8%, p=0.04) but had no significant effect among smokers (16.5% vs 14.5%, p=0.4).

For intention to smoke, the advertisement did not significantly change non-smokers' intentions (1.2% vs 1.6%, p=0.54), but smokers in the intervention group were more likely to say they would be smoking in 12 months than controls (38.6% vs 25.6%, p<0.001).
The study included 3091 cinema patrons aged 12-24 in Australia, with 18.6% current smokers, surveyed after a movie in a quasi-experimental design.
Thus, it affected young people's perceptions only among non-smokers and did not reduce smoking intention, with an unexpected higher intention among smokers.
The evidence is mixed: overall self-reported competence was broadly similar between rural and urban midwives, but specific competencies differed by location.

In a Scottish survey of 82 remote/rural and 107 urban midwives (response rates 85% vs 60%), rural midwives were more likely to report competence in breech delivery (p=0.001), while urban midwives more often reported competence in intravenous fluid replacement and newborn examination (both p<0.001).
Thus rural location is associated with differences in some competencies, not a uniform overall effect.
Yes, the study reports gender differences in the factors associated with delay, though the overall median delay difference between women and men was not significant.
In 61 African American men and women diagnosed with AMI across five hospitals, median prehospital delay was longer for women than men (4.4 vs 3.5 hours) but not significantly so.
For women, being single or alone when symptoms began was associated with longer delays, and receiving advice to seek help or call 911 was associated with shorter delays.
For men, being at home, having emergency room insurance, and using transportation other than an ambulance were associated with longer delays.
Thus, the correlates of delay differed by gender in this sample.
The evidence is mixed: a statistically significant but clinically weak relationship was found, while the difference across ACE quartiles was not significant.
In 300 people with Type 1 diabetes not taking renin-angiotensin system blockers, the incidence of severe hypoglycaemia was 0.93 episodes per patient year.

The mean incidence of severe hypoglycaemia in the top versus bottom quartiles of ACE activity was 0.5 versus 1.7 episodes per patient year, but this difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.075).

Spearman's test showed a very weak but statistically significant association between serum ACE and severe hypoglycaemia incidence (r = 0.115, P = 0.047), and a negative binomial model also showed a statistically significant but clinically weak relationship (P = 0.002).
Yes—teaching text comprehension strategies improved general reading comprehension in adults with mild intellectual disability, with substantial transfer effects that were maintained at follow-up.
The study included 38 adults aged 20–72 years (mean age 36) with ID and IQs of 45–69 (mean IQ 58), who received 15 weekly 1-hour lessons over 3 months.
There was no significant difference between individual instruction and small-group reciprocal teaching instruction conditions.
Direct strategy-test effects were substantial except for questioning, and the transfer effect to general text comprehension was even more substantial.
No, family history was not reliable for choosing which school children to screen in the supplied study.
Among 2096 school children in Ankara (1043 male, 1053 female; mean age 9.03 years), 135 had serum cholesterol ≥200 mg/dL and 83 had LDL-cholesterol ≥130 mg/dL.
Although 64.4% reported a family history of hyperlipidemia, no relations were found between family history and serum lipid levels.

The evidence is mixed: in locally advanced urothelial carcinoma patients receiving adjuvant M-VEC, HER2 immunoreactivity was a significant prognostic factor for progression-free survival (p=0.03) and disease-specific overall survival (p=0.02) by univariate analysis but not by multivariate analysis.

In the overall advanced urothelial carcinoma cohort, HER2 immunoreactivity was significantly associated with PFS (p=0.02) and disease-specific OS (p=0.005), while nodal status was a strong independent prognostic indicator.
The study evaluated 114 formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded specimens from patients receiving surgery alone or adjuvant M-VEC, and HER2 was not prognostic for patients receiving watchful waiting.

No, it is not just a difference between the rich and the poor, because maternal mortality audit identified different causes of and contributing factors to deaths in different low- and high-income settings.
The study compared rural populations in Zambia and The Gambia, a peri-urban population in Namibia, and nationwide data from the Netherlands.
The maternal mortality ratio ranged from 10 per 100,000 in the Netherlands to 1540 per 100,000 in The Gambia.
Causes differed across settings, with HIV/AIDS in Namibia, sepsis and HIV/AIDS in Zambia, (pre-)eclampsia in the Netherlands, and obstructed labour in The Gambia.
Yes, the evidence suggests that postoperative pain level can be predicted preoperatively, based on significant correlations with several preoperative factors.

In a prospective study of 86 patients over 18 years old undergoing shoulder surgery, preoperative data included past history of pain, intensity and duration of prior pain, triggering factors, localization, and psychological context.
Postoperative pain intensity was measured on a visual analog scale up to 24 hours postoperatively and then at one month.
Significant postoperative pain was correlated with a prior history of surgical pain, duration of prior pain, intensity of preoperative pain, and depression.
Yes—adjuvant aromatase inhibitors are associated with a modestly increased risk of grade 3/4 cardiovascular events compared with tamoxifen in early breast cancer trials.

In a meta-analysis of 7 randomized trials including 19,818 patients, the absolute difference in cardiovascular adverse events was 0.52%, with RR 1.31 (95% CI 1.07–1.60; P=.007) and NNH 189; for third-generation AIs, RR was 1.34 (95% CI 1.09–1.63; P=.0038).
The same analysis found thromboembolic events were significantly less frequent with AIs than tamoxifen (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.42–0.65; P<.0001).
The passages do not explicitly state that the trial populations were postmenopausal, although they describe adjuvant AI versus tamoxifen trials in early breast cancer.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether surgical management is necessary.

In a retrospective review of 56 patients with nonpalpable testis and spermatic vessels and vas deferens exiting a closed internal inguinal ring, 8 testicular remnants (14%) had viable germ cell elements and 4 (7%) had seminiferous tubules without germ cell elements.
The passages do not compare surgery with observation or report clinical outcomes, so they do not settle whether removal is necessary.

Yes, body diffusion-weighted MR imaging is helpful for detecting uterine endometrial cancer when added to nonenhanced MR imaging, increasing sensitivity from 83% to 96% in one study. In 23 patients with endometrial cancer, T2-weighted images alone detected cancers in 19 of 23 (83%). Adding DW images and fused DW/T2-weighted images identified cancers in 3 of the remaining 4 patients, for overall detection sensitivity of 96%. The mean ADC of endometrial cancer (n=22) was (0.97+/-0.19)x10(-3) mm2/s, significantly lower than normal endometrium, myometrium, leiomyoma, and adenomyosis (p<0.05).
The evidence is mixed: topical ropivacaine reduces post-tonsillectomy pain after the first hour but does not reduce other morbidity in pediatric patients.

In a prospective, randomized, double-blind trial of 41 children aged 4–16 years undergoing tonsillectomy, 1.0% ropivacaine-soaked swabs in the tonsillar fossae significantly reduced pain in the other hours and days compared with saline-soaked swabs (p<0.001), but not during the first hour (p>0.05).
Nausea, fever, vomiting, odor, bleeding, otalgia, and trismus were not statistically different between groups, and no ropivacaine-related complications or systemic side effects occurred.
Yes—pectin content and low-methylated pectin increased with cold acclimation and most cold-induced cell-wall changes were reversed by de-acclimation in winter oil-seed rape.
The evidence comes from leaves of two double-haploid lines of Brassica napus subsp. oleifera differing in winter survival and blackleg resistance.

Cold acclimation at 2°C retarded leaf expansion and increased freezing resistance, leaf tensile stiffness, cell wall and pectin contents, pectin methylesterase activity, and low-methylated pectin content independently of genotype, though changes were more pronounced in the more pathogen-resistant genotype.
De-acclimation promoted leaf expansion and reversed most cold-induced effects except pectin methylesterase activity.
Yes, routine laboratory markers appear useful for differentiating nonalcoholic from alcoholic steatohepatitis.

In 95 patients with steatohepatitis (58 NASH, 37 ASH), MCV was elevated in 53% of ASH patients but normal in all NASH patients (P<0.0001), and an AST/ALT ratio >1 was more common in ASH (54.1% vs 20.7%, P=0.0008).
Multivariate analysis identified MCV, AST/ALT ratio, and sex as relevant regressors, with an aROC of 0.92.
No—the evidence suggests that specialized phonological awareness training is not clearly indicated for every preschool child, because it did not produce a substantial benefit in the whole group.

In a prospective study, 218 preschool children were assigned to either specialized phonological awareness training to prevent dyslexia or general perception training, and 131 were later compared in first grade for reading and writing.
In the whole group, only a slight difference was found between the two training modalities for writing abilities.
However, children with a history of hearing loss, current hearing loss, or pathologic middle ear findings profited most from the specialized program in reading compared with controls.
Thus, the passages support targeted use in hearing-risk children rather than universal specialized training for all preschoolers.
The evidence is insufficient to say whether chest wall irradiation should be included after mastectomy in node-negative breast cancer.

A retrospective analysis of 92 node-negative breast cancer patients with internal or central tumors treated with mastectomy and external irradiation of the internal mammary chain only (50 Gy) reported a 5% local recurrence rate (5 cases), with recurrences at the operative scar and chest wall.
Risk factors for local failure were age <=40 years and tumor size >20 mm, without statistical significance.
These passages do not compare chest wall irradiation with no chest wall irradiation, so they do not settle whether it should be included.
No, low-tone sudden deafness does not inevitably progress to Meniere's disease.

In a retrospective review of 184 patients with low-tone SD, 83 of 177 patients without vertigo had recurrent hearing loss and 15 of those 83 developed vertiginous attacks, while the remaining 94 had a single episode.

Among seven patients with low-tone SD accompanied by vertigo, three had recurrent hearing loss and two of the three were subsequently confirmed to have Meniere's disease, while the other four had a single episode.
The study found no difference in the rate of progression from SD to Meniere's disease between the low-tone and high-tone SD groups.
The evidence is insufficient to establish a diagnostic role for c-kit in HBV-related liver disease, because the study reports expression patterns and prevalence but no diagnostic accuracy measures.

In 125 HBV-infected patients grouped as mild, moderate, or severe hepatitis, cirrhosis, and HCC (25 each), plus 50 additional HBV-related HCCs, c-kit immunohistochemistry showed the greatest positivity and staining intensity in severe hepatitis and HCC, with staining intensity paralleling grade and stage in chronic hepatitis B.
C-kit positivity was rare or absent in fibrotic areas and cirrhotic liver, while 62 of 75 HCC specimens (82%) were positive (p<0.001).
These findings show an association with disease severity and HCC but do not settle whether c-kit has diagnostic utility.
Yes—higher Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits were linked to lower disability rates among the elderly.
The study used 1990 and 2000 census data and state/year fixed-effect models to test whether within-state changes in maximum SSI benefits led to changes in disability among people aged 65 and older.
Among all single elderly individuals, 30% had mobility limitations, and a $100 per month increase in the maximum SSI benefit caused the mobility limitation rate to fall by 0.46 percentage points.

Effects were larger among those most likely to receive SSI and absent among those least likely to receive SSI, and the findings were robust to sensitivity analyses, Medicaid confounding, and for married individuals.
The evidence is insufficient to show that confined placental mosaicism accounts for adverse perinatal outcomes in IVF pregnancies.

In a retrospective CVS study, the incidence of CPM was not significantly higher in IVF/ICSI pregnancies than in spontaneous conceptions (1.3% vs 2.2%; OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.19–1.85), while fetal chromosomal anomalies were also not significantly increased (4.3% vs 2.4%; OR 1.81, 95% CI 0.95–3.42).
The study population comprised 20,885 CVS results, including 235 IVF/ICSI and 20,650 control pregnancies, and it did not directly assess perinatal outcomes or link CPM to them.

Yes, laparoscopic surgery was associated with a decreased risk of new-onset atrial fibrillation after major foregut surgery in a retrospective study of 154 adults. In that study, 14 of 154 patients developed new-onset atrial fibrillation, and laparoscopic surgery (p = 0.004) and nonthoracic surgery (p = 0.01) were associated with lower risk. Multivariate analysis adjusting for surgery type showed atrial fibrillation was associated with older age (OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02–1.14, p = 0.01) and inversely associated with laparoscopic surgery (OR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01–0.95, p = 0.04).
No, the evidence indicates wandering and physically nonaggressive agitation (PNA) are not equivalent, based on differing factor structures and only moderate-to-low correlations.
In 181 ambulatory residents with DSM-IV dementia from 22 nursing homes and 6 assisted living facilities, videotaped observations were coded for wandering and six PNA behaviors.
Factor analyses yielded a one-factor solution for wandering (43.66% variance explained) and a two-factor solution for PNA (53.45% variance explained).
Overall wandering correlated with PNA Factor 1 at r=0.68 and with Factor 2 at r=0.26.
Thus the constructs are related but not equivalent.

The evidence is mixed/insufficient to conclude that it is better to be big, because an evaluation of a Swedish hospital merger found only a moderate quality increase and did not clearly show the hoped-for economic gains.
The evaluation surveyed 597 randomly selected employees (24% of health care staff) at Blekinge Hospital; 498 responded (83%), and interviews were also conducted.
The passages do not report a direct comparison of bigger versus smaller hospitals.
A moderate increase in quality was assessed, but a low proportion of employees perceived it had decisively or largely to do with the merger.
The majority perceived economic incentives as drivers of change, but only 10% of that group believed the target was reached completely or to a large extent.

Yes—robotically assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy (RALP) appears less invasive than radical retropubic prostatectomy (RRP) in this study, because RRP produced greater rises in acute-phase markers. In 35 RALP and 26 RRP patients, baseline IL-1, IL-6, CRP and lactate were comparable. Mean IL-6 and CRP were higher for RRP at T1–T4 (P values 0.01 to <0.001), and lactate was higher for RRP at T2–T4 (P = 0.001 to 0.004). IL-1 alpha did not change at the sampled times.
No—Kell alloimmunization was not associated with clinically significant fetal thrombocytopenia, although mild thrombocytopenia occurred in 10%.

In a retrospective cohort of 42 pregnancies with severe Kell alloimmunization, fetal thrombocytopenia (platelet count <150 x 10^9/L) was found in 4/42 (10%), compared with 84/318 (26%) in RhD alloimmunized controls.

None of the Kell fetuses, including 15 with severe hydrops, had clinically significant thrombocytopenia (<50 x 10^9/L), whereas 2/230 (1%) non-hydropic and 7/30 (23%) severely hydropic RhD fetuses did.
Thus the evidence does not support an association between Kell alloimmunization and clinically significant fetal thrombocytopenia, though mild thrombocytopenia can occur.
The evidence is mixed: longer radiotherapy treatment duration was associated with worse biochemical control in some analyses but not others.

Among 1,796 men with prostate cancer treated with radiotherapy alone, a higher nontreatment day ratio (NTDR ≥33% vs <33%) was linked to lower 10-year freedom from biochemical failure overall (58% vs 68%, p=0.02) and in low-risk disease (57% vs 82%, p=0.0019), and NTDR was independently predictive on multivariate analysis (p=0.03).
However, NTDR was not a significant predictor in intermediate-risk, high-risk, or all risk groups combined.
Yes—physician specialty significantly influenced both the frequency and depth of medication-history documentation in patients' case notes.

The evidence comes from a cross-sectional assessment of 123 physicians documenting medication histories for 900 randomly selected patients stratified across nine specialties (Cardiology, Chest, Dermatology, Endocrine, Gastroenterology, Haematology, Neurology, Psychiatry, and Renal) at a 900-bed teaching hospital in Ibadan, Nigeria.
Physicians' specialties significantly influenced the depth of documentation (P<0.0001) and the frequency of documentation (P<0.0001) across the nine specialties.
The evidence is insufficient to determine whether specialty pharmaceuticals are worth their price, because the available pharmacoeconomic data are not robust enough to establish value.

The passages describe these agents as promising increased life expectancy, improved quality of life, enhanced workplace productivity, decreased disease burden, and reduced health care spending, but note they come at significant cost and require special handling, administration, patient education, clinical support, risk mitigation, and controlled distribution.
They provide no population, comparator, or numerical cost-effectiveness estimates, so they do not settle the worth question.

No, the supplied evidence suggests hormonal differences are not responsible for the gender dimorphism: female gender was independently associated with a 43% lower risk of multiple organ failure and a 23% lower risk of nosocomial infection, and this protection remained unchanged in young (<48 years) versus old (>52 years) women.
The cohort included 1,036 blunt-injured adults with hemorrhagic shock (680 men, 356 women) and used Cox regression controlling for confounders.
The passages do not directly measure hormones; they use reproductive age as a proxy and show that the female advantage persists across age groups, arguing against an age-related hormonal explanation.

Yes, the evidence suggests a role for ADRB gene polymorphisms in TTN: among 73 term TTN newborns and 55 healthy Caucasian controls, the beta1Ser49Gly polymorphism differed significantly, and beta1Gly49 homozygotes had higher TTN risk than beta1Ser49 allele carriers (OR 18.5; 95% CI 1.5-229; p=0.023).
A T-47C, A46G, C79G, and C491T (TACC) haplotype in ADRB2 was also significantly associated with TTN (p=0.048).
The findings are limited by the small sample size and wide confidence interval, so they support but do not definitively establish a role.

The evidence is suggestive but not conclusive that bezafibrate prevents colon cancer in patients with coronary artery disease; in the randomized BIP study, colon cancer occurred in 8/1506 (0.53%) on bezafibrate vs 17/1505 (1.13%) on placebo, with a one-sided p=0.05 and two-sided p=0.07. The population was 3011 patients without any cancer diagnosis enrolled in the double-blind Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention (BIP) Study, randomized to 400 mg bezafibrate retard or placebo daily. On multivariable analysis, the hazard ratio for colon cancer with bezafibrate was 0.47 (95% CI 0.2–1.1), and a difference was only detectable after a 4-year lag and progressively increased with continued follow-up. Thus, the passages show a trend toward lower colon cancer incidence but do not establish a statistically significant preventive effect.
Yes—intradialytic endothelin-1 (ET-1) changes differed by hemodynamic status, decreasing with dialysis-induced hypotension and increasing with rebound hypertension.

In 45 ESRD patients on regular hemodialysis divided into stable hemodynamics, dialysis-induced hypotension, and rebound hypertension groups, plus 15 healthy controls, post-dialysis ET-1 was unchanged in the stable group (14.49 +/- 2.04 vs.
14.33 +/- 2.23 pg/ml; P = NS), decreased in the hypotension group (8.56 +/- 1.44 vs.
11.75 +/- 2.51 pg/ml; P<0.001), and increased in the rebound hypertension group (16.39 +/- 3.12 vs.
11.93 +/- 2.11 pg/ml; P<0.001) compared with predialysis values.
Pre-dialysis ET-1 levels were significantly higher in dialysis patients than controls (P<0.001) but comparable among the three hemodialysis groups.
Yes, severe macrosomia appears to be manifested at 11–14 weeks of gestation, based on a case-control study showing greater measured-than-expected crown-rump length in affected pregnancies.

In 30 term severely macrosomic neonates versus 90 appropriate-for-gestational-age controls, the difference between measured and expected CRL at nuchal translucency screening was significantly larger in macrosomic cases (mean 6.66 ± 4.78 mm vs 1.17 ± 4.6 mm, P<0.0001; and 3 ± 2.2 days vs 0.5 ± 2.3 days, P<0.0001).
The study also found significant correlations between the extent of macrosomia and the CRL discrepancy (r=0.47, P<0.01 and r=0.48, P<0.01).
Yes, the ability to perform transurethral resection of the prostate appears influenced by the surgeon's previous experience, based on a higher rate of tissue resection by a senior urologist.

In a study of 67 patients undergoing TURP without a video camera, patients were randomly allocated to three groups according to surgeon experience: a urologist having done 25 TURPs (24 patients), one having done 50 TURPs (24 patients), and a senior urologist with vast TURP experience (19 patients).

The weight of resected tissue per minute was approximately four times higher in the senior group than in the two less-experienced groups, although mean absorbed irrigation fluid was similar (p=0.24) and TUR syndrome occurred in 4 patients (6%) with no significant difference between groups.
Yes—refusers differed from participants in some characteristics.

In older patients from a Dutch outpatient clinic invited to a self-management intervention, 267 of 361 (74%) refused, and refusers were more restricted in mobility, lived farther from the intervention location, and more often had a partner than participants.
No differences were found in education, age, or gender; main refusal reasons were lack of time, travel distance, and transport problems.

No; in a prospective cohort of 909 participants with major depressive and bipolar disorders followed through 4204 mood cycles, the effects of risk factors for suicidal behavior did not differ by affective disorder polarity.

The modeled risk factors were age, gender, hopelessness, married status, prior suicide attempts, and active substance abuse; age, hopelessness, and active substance abuse, but not polarity, predicted suicidal behavior.

During follow-up, 40 cycles ended in suicide and 384 cycles contained at least one suicide attempt, and after controlling for age of onset, prior suicide attempts did not differ by polarity, although bipolar participants had more prior severe attempts.
Thus, the study found no differential effects of risk factors by polarity.
Yes, there is a relationship: serum homocysteine was significantly higher in patients with vitiligo than in healthy controls.
In 26 vitiligo patients and 26 age-matched controls, mean serum homocysteine was 21.61 ± 13.28 vs.
Homocysteine level was also related to disease activity and was significantly higher in progressive vitiligo than in controls (25.4 ± 14.99 vs.

Yes, a geriatric oncology consultation modified the cancer treatment plan in a substantial proportion of elderly patients. In a study of 105 patients aged 70 or older referred to a geriatric oncology consultation, among the 93 with an initial treatment decision, the plan was modified in 38.7% after assessment. Only body mass index and the absence of depressive symptoms were associated with a modification of the treatment plan.
No, in this study, mailing surgeons a one-page summary of current evidence did not significantly change their practice of prophylactic nasogastric decompression.

The study compared elective colonic resection patients at the Royal Alexandra Hospital before the intervention (October-November 2004) with patients after all general surgeons were mailed the evidence summary (January-February 2005).
Prophylactic NG decompression was used in 7 of 22 pre-intervention cases versus 5 of 21 post-intervention cases, and the difference was not statistically significant.
This single study therefore does not show that familiarization with current evidence changed practice, though it directly tested that question in this setting.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia has the same evolution as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.
The study was designed to ascertain whether vaginal lesions have a natural history similar to cervical lesions.

It found that among patients with mild vaginal lesions, mild cervical lesions were significantly more frequent than severe cervical lesions, and among patients with "active" vaginal lesions, "active" cervical lesions were significantly more frequent than "non active" cervical lesions.

However, differences in rates of mild and severe cervical lesions among patients with high-grade versus low-grade VAIN (with and without koilocytosis) were not significant, and VAIN may be related to risk factors different from simple HPV infections.

No—overweight children do not necessarily become overweight adults, based on Japanese female growth curves showing that more recent birth cohorts were more overweight as children but thinner as young women.
The study compared BMI growth curves from childhood to young adulthood in 76,635 females aged 1–25 years using retrospective repeated cross-sectional annual nationwide surveys from 1948 to 2005.

More recent cohorts had larger BMI increments in early childhood but smaller adolescent increments and earlier, lower-peak BMI declines in young adults, resulting in lower BMI as young women than older cohorts.
However, these are cross-sectional cohort comparisons, not individual tracking, so they do not establish individual-level transition probabilities.
Yes, cytokines appear to have a role in epilepsy, based on detectable serum cytokine levels in patients and their decrease during seizure-free periods.

In a prospective study of 100 patients with epilepsy or new-onset seizure compared with 100 matched healthy controls, detectable serum cytokines included IL-6 (42), TNF-alpha (36), IL-2 (22), IL-4 (22), IFN-gamma (20), and IL-1 (11).
Correlations were noted between status epilepticus and IL-6 (p=0.04) and between more than one year history of epilepsy and IL-1beta (p=0.02).
In 16 patients sampled again during the seizure-free period, levels decreased for TNF-alpha (25% to 12.5%), IFN-gamma (12.5% to 0%), IL-1 (25% to 0%), IL-4 (18.8% to 0%), and IL-6 (18.8% to 6.2%).
However, this shows associations and not proof of causality.

Yes, but only for certain IBD subgroups: calprotectin predicted relapse in ulcerative colitis (UC) and colonic Crohn's disease (CD), not all CD. In a prospective study of 97 UC and 65 CD patients in clinical remission, a positive stool calprotectin test (cutoff 130 mg/kg) was significantly associated with 1-year relapse in UC (26/44 positive vs 11/53 negative relapsed; P=0.000). Among CD patients overall, 13/30 positive vs 7/35 negative relapsed, but the significant correlation was reported only for colonic CD (4/6 positive relapsed; P=0.02). The passages therefore support calprotectin as a relapse predictor in UC and colonic CD, but do not establish it for all CD.
Yes—myometrial electrical activity, measured as electrical uterine myography (EUM), can help identify true preterm labor and predict preterm delivery within 14 days.

In a prospective study of 87 women at less than 35 weeks' gestation, an EUM index score based on contraction period, peak power, and center-of-activity movement was compared with fetal fibronectin and cervical length.
Patients who delivered within 14 days had a higher EUM index and mean RMS (P =.000), and no patients with EUM index scores of 1–2 delivered in that timeframe.

Combining EUM with cervical length or fetal fibronectin increased predictability, and logistic regression showed a 4- to 5-fold increased risk of preterm delivery with prior preterm delivery history and EUM index.
These findings support its use for identifying patients in preterm labor, though the evidence comes from a small prospective study.
Evidence from this single study suggests octogenarians are not at high risk for carotid endarterectomy, with no deaths and low perioperative neurologic complications.

In 103 carotid endarterectomies performed on 95 octogenarians (ages 80-89), there were 4 perioperative neurologic complications: 1 transient ischemic attack (0.97%), 2 minor strokes (1.94%), and 1 major stroke (0.97%), with no deaths.
However, the background notes that it has been proposed that being an octogenarian places patients in a high-risk category, and the passages do not provide a direct comparison to younger patients.

Yes—post-treatment fear of recurrence in head and neck cancer survivors was directly predicted by pre-treatment fear of recurrence and optimism, but not by demographic, disease, treatment, or symptom factors. In a prospective study of 82 newly diagnosed head and neck cancer patients (54 males, 28 females, mean age 60 years), fears of recurrence were measured before treatment and 6–8 months after treatment. At diagnosis, one third reported relatively high fear of recurrence, and 12% still reported similar levels 6–8 months after treatment. Path analyses showed that fears after treatment were directly predicted by pre-treatment fears and optimism, while fears were unrelated to any socio-demographic or disease/treatment/symptom-related factors.

Yes—home sampling kits for multiple bacterial STIs were generally viewed as acceptable among men who have sex with men in a qualitative study, though concerns were raised. The finding rests on focus groups with 20 MSM and one-to-one interviews with 24 MSM, some of whom had experience with self-sampling in a pilot clinical study. Participants identified benefits such as increased access to testing, enhanced personal comfort and empowerment, but also concerns about test accuracy, delays in receiving results, possible lack of support, and potential negative impact on others.
The evidence is mixed/qualified: ACMIA correlated closely with MEIA (r=0.84) with no specific Bland-Altman trend, but the ACMIA-MEIA difference tended to be larger in low-hematocrit samples (P<.001).
The comparison used 154 samples from kidney or liver transplant recipients, measuring tacrolimus by Dimension RxL HM ACMIA and IMx tacrolimus II MEIA.

Both methods' tacrolimus levels were not influenced by hematocrit, yet the hematocrit-dependent between-method difference means the passages do not fully establish ACMIA as an unconditional alternative to MEIA.
The evidence is insufficient to establish a causative link between probable Say-Barber-Miller syndrome and cerebro-mediastinal tuberculosis.

The report describes a seven-year-old girl with probable Say-Barber-Miller syndrome (facial dysmorphy, microcephaly, mental retardation, recurrent infections) who presented with a mediastinal mass involving the spine and cerebral tuberculomas, with a positive tuberculin reaction and vertebral biopsy culture positive for Koch bacillus.
An extensive immunological work-up was normal, and the authors discuss a putative causative link without comparative or mechanistic evidence.
Thus, the passages show co-occurrence and a hypothesis, but they do not settle whether the syndrome caused the tuberculosis.
Yes, the zeolite hemostatic agent decreased total blood loss in a swine extremity arterial injury model.

In this study, 16 swine with a lacerated femoral artery were allocated to a control group (n=6) treated with a pressure dressing and manual pressure or a QuikClot group (n=10) treated by direct application of QuikClot.
The QuikClot group also had a slower drop in blood pressure and significantly higher hematocrit levels, though the agent generated significant heat and mild nerve changes were observed.
The evidence is insufficient to confirm "Main Gate Syndrome" as a new format in mass-casualty surge management.
The passages describe a single experience of 14 casualties from suicide bombings in Afghanistan, with a first triage by a U.S.
Army Level I group, a second surgical triage with ultrasound, and four cases (ISS>25) re-categorized for emergency surgery.
They do not use the term "Main Gate Syndrome" or compare this approach to other surge management formats.
No, quantitative left ventricular regional wall motion did not change after fibrous tissue resection in patients with endomyocardial fibrosis.

In a prospective study of 30 patients (20 female, 30±10 years) evaluated before and 5±8 months after surgery, left ventricular wall motion in five regions did not differ between pre- and postoperative measurements.
Regional motion was measured by the centerline method and expressed in standard deviation units from a normal reference population, and the left ventricular ejection fraction also did not change.
NYHA functional class improved, but that is separate from regional wall motion.
No, in this single study only 11 of 835 colorectal cancers (1.3%) were estimated to have been missed in the adenoma phase, so many cancers were not attributable to missed adenomas.
Among 835 patients diagnosed with colorectal cancer over 15 years, 25 had undergone a previous endoscopy without a cancer diagnosis.
Of those 25, only 11 had no argument for regular follow-up, and assuming their cancers developed from an adenoma, the missed-adenoma rate was 11/835 (1.3%).
The background notes that the number of colorectal cancers due to missed adenomas is unknown and the literature is sparse, so this estimate may not be definitive.
The evidence is insufficient to call cyanoacrylate a reliable alternative in clinical practice, although it performed well in an experimental rat model.

In 96 Sprague-Dawley rats, intestinal anastomoses performed with ethyl-2-cyanoacrylate had no significant difference in bursting pressures compared with polyglactin 910 sutures on postoperative days 2 and 6, while hydroxyproline levels and anastomosis time were significantly better in the cyanoacrylate group.
These findings support comparable strength and better healing/operation time in rats, but they do not demonstrate reliability in humans.

The evidence is mixed: in a neurovascular clinic cohort, older patients (>75 years) had similar time from symptom onset to clinic appointment (median 24 days vs 24 days) and no differences in prescribed secondary preventive treatments compared with younger patients (≤75 years), but they received less MRI (4% vs 26%) and carotid Doppler imaging (77% vs 92%) and less advice on weight reduction (12.9% vs 30.2%) and diet (31.7% vs 46.3%). Older patients also experienced less delay for carotid endarterectomy (49 vs 90 days), while younger patients had scans performed more quickly. The passages do not define a standard for adequate stroke care or report clinical outcomes, so they cannot fully settle whether older patients receive adequate care overall.

No—on multivariate analysis the growth rate was not related to the neoplastic nature of a gallbladder polyp, although a rapid growth rate (>0.6 mm/mo) was more common in neoplastic polyps univariately.

In 145 patients with GB polyps followed by ultrasound before cholecystectomy (125 non-neoplastic, 20 neoplastic), neoplastic polyps were more frequent with age >60 years, hypertension, size >10 mm, and growth >0.6 mm/mo.
However, only older age (>60 y) and large size (>10 mm) remained significantly associated with neoplastic polyps on multivariate analysis.
The evidence is insufficient to say a better predictive model was validated, but the observed epidemiology suggests current readiness assumptions can be better calibrated.

In 32 Israeli terrorism attacks from November 2000 to June 2003, there were 62 HMCIs and 1292 casualties; mean casualties per hospital were 20.8±13.3 (range 4–56, median 16.5), and 95% of HMCIs had ≤52 casualties.

Because 1022/1292 (79.2%) did not require immediate treatment, the guideline expectation that half need immediate care is not supported, but the passages do not show a validated method for predicting surge capacity or severity distribution.
The evidence is mixed: MRI does not accurately predict concordant pain provocation overall, although one combined finding is highly specific.
In 62 patients with axial low back pain likely disc-related, 178 discs were tested by discography and MRI findings were correlated with concordant pain.
Disc protrusion with high-intensity zone correlated significantly with concordant pain (P<0.01), with specificity 97.8% and positive predictive value 87.0%, but sensitivity was only 45.5%.
Disc degeneration, disc protrusion alone, and high-intensity zone alone were not helpful for identifying a disc with concordant pain.

Yes, the determination between complete and incomplete traumatic spinal cord injury is clinically relevant, as the currently used complete/incomplete classification significantly predicted 1-year independent ambulation in 432 patients with traumatic SCI.
In that study, the complete/incomplete distinction had an AUC of 0.823 (P<0.001, 95% CI 0.781-0.864) for prognosing independent ambulation 1 year post injury.
However, a combination of voluntary anal contraction and S4-5 light touch and pin prick scores was significantly better (AUC 0.906, P<0.001, 95% CI 0.871-0.941).
No, the ADAM questionnaire is not useful for screening partial androgen deficiency of aging men (PADAM) because it had high sensitivity (83.3%) but very low specificity (19.7%) in this study.
In a cross-sectional study of 96 men aged 40 or older in Santiago, Chile, 81.3% screened positive on ADAM, but only 28.1% had PADAM confirmed by available testosterone <198.4 ng/dL.
Item 1 (decreased sexual desire) was a better predictor than the complete questionnaire, with 63.3% sensitivity and 66.7% specificity.

The evidence is mixed: among 20 ambulatory children with spina bifida, peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) from graded treadmill testing did not differ significantly from VO2 during a supramaximal protocol, but 5 children improved during supramaximal testing, indicating VO2peak may not reflect true maximum oxygen uptake for all.
Fifteen of the 20 children met at least 2 of 3 criteria for maximum exercise testing, and one failed to meet any, further suggesting most but not all reached maximal effort.
Average VO2peak was 1.23 L/min (SD=0.6) and 34.1 mL/kg/min (SD=8.3).
These findings apply to children with spina bifida who are at least community ambulatory.
Yes for primary sternal closure in a human cadaver model, but the passages do not directly address secondary closure.

In 18 cadavers, the intrathoracic pressure needed to cause 2.0 mm sternal separation increased from 183.3 +/- 123.9 with wires/cables alone to 301.4 +/- 204.5 with wires/cables plus one plate and to 355.0 +/- 210.4 with four plates alone (p<0.05), with regression coefficients of 120 (95% CI 47-194) and 142 (66-219) for the plate groups.
The study tested closure after midline sternotomy, not secondary closure for mediastinitis, so it supports improved stability for primary closure in this model but leaves secondary closure unproven.

The evidence is insufficient to determine whether UK radiologists are satisfied with the training and support received in suspected child abuse, because the survey did not directly assess satisfaction with training or support.

In a survey of consultant radiologists from 84 UK departments, 61% thought the service could be improved, 5% provided expert evidence, and 73% would never consider providing expert evidence even if given adequate radiology and/or legal training.
These findings do not directly measure satisfaction with training or support, so they do not settle the question.
No; in eight chronic hemodialysis patients, oral sodium bicarbonate increased blood pH from 7.41 to 7.46 (p = 0.041) but did not significantly stimulate protein synthesis.
The fractional synthesis rates of muscle protein (2.1 +/- 0.2 vs.
2.0 +/- 0.5% per day, p = 0.39) and albumin (8.3 +/- 2.2 vs.
8.6 +/- 2.5% per day, p = 0.31) were not significantly changed after 10-14 days of supplementation.

The evidence is insufficient to show that foreign bodies migrate through the body towards the heart, because although the passages mention a popular saying that 'FB walk to the heart,' the documented migrations went to the aorta, neck, prevertebral fascia, and submandibular region rather than the heart.
In a 40-year sample of 3,000 foreign bodies, four had extra-lumen migration.

Three clinical histories described two fish bones and one piece of fish cartilage; migration started in the esophagus in two (one to the aorta, one to the neck area) and in the pharynx in two (one to the prevertebral fascia, one externalized in the submandibular region).
Thus, the passages show that foreign bodies can migrate outside the lumen but do not establish migration toward the heart.

Yes, the evidence suggests ESC can change the way some people drive, based on self-reported long-lasting changes in driving behavior among ESC owners. In a Canadian survey of 1,017 owners/drivers of 2006–2008 ESC-equipped passenger vehicles, 23% of those who knew their vehicle had ESC reported noticing long-lasting changes in their driving behavior since they began driving it. The study also found that 90% of drivers who knew their vehicle had ESC believed it made driving safer and were confident it would work in an emergency, though the objective was to assess whether behavioral adaptation is likely rather than to measure actual driving changes.

No, they are not consistently documented: among 84 MMT patients, opioid dependence documentation was missing from the medical record in 30% (95% CI, 20%-41%) and MMT documentation was missing from the last primary care note or hospital discharge summary in 11% (95% CI, 5%-19%).
The study reviewed electronic medical records of patients from a methadone clinic who received primary care from an affiliated but separate medical center.
No—in a longitudinal study of Danish healthcare workers, the relationship between transformational leadership and sleep quality was not mediated by self-efficacy.

The study used structural equation modelling with 447 workers at baseline in 2005 and 274 at 18-month follow-up in 2007, finding direct relationships between transformational leadership and sleep quality.

These direct relationships were negative cross-sectionally at both time points but positive between baseline and follow-up, while self-efficacy did not mediate the leadership–sleep quality relationship.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that single-valve replacement is safe in patients with both mitral and aortic prostheses and active prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE).
In a series of 20 such patients, 17 underwent surgery and 13 had only the valve that seemed infected replaced.
Among those 13, 4 died within a week after the procedure, while 9 survived, completed antimicrobial therapy, and were considered cured without relapse over a mean follow-up of 15.78 months.

No, prostate specific antigen does not appear to need adjustment for body mass index, based on a longitudinal aging study finding no significant association after age adjustment. In 994 men without prostate cancer (4,937 observations), a 10-point BMI increase was associated with a PSA difference of only -0.03 ng/ml (95% CI -0.40-0.49), and the age-adjusted association was not significant (p = 0.06). Results were similar when men with prostate cancer were included, when percent body fat replaced BMI, and after adjusting for prostate volume, and longitudinal weight changes also had no significant association with PSA.
No, the survey evidence indicates there is no consensus among breast surgeons on attaining negative margins in breast-conservation operations, as answers showed a large variety in clinical practices.
Among 1,000 surveyed surgeons interested in breast cancer treatment, 381 responded and 351 were analyzed.
Acceptable negative margins varied widely: 15% would accept any negative margin, 28% a 1-mm margin, 50% a 2-mm margin, 12% a 5-mm margin, and 3% a 10-mm margin.
Reexcision decisions also differed, with 57% never reexcising for a positive deep margin while 53% always reexcising for a positive anterior margin.
No.

In a prospective randomized trial of 104 patients with choledocholithiasis-induced acute cholangitis who underwent primary endoscopic treatment, routine ENBD after CBD stone clearance did not reduce cholangitis recurrence at 24 weeks (3.9% vs 3.8%; P =.99) or shorten hospital stay (7.9 vs 7.9 days; P =.98) compared with no ENBD.
ENBD was associated with longer procedure time (26.2 vs 22.7 minutes; P =.01) and higher discomfort score (4.9 vs 2.8; P =.02).
Thus, the evidence does not support routine nasobiliary drainage insertion in this setting.

Yes, the evidence supports biomolecular identification as a new perspective for aerobiological monitoring, based on a study that tested a real-time PCR approach as an alternative to morphologic identification.

The study modified a CTAB-based DNA extraction protocol to obtain good-quality pollen DNA, identified taxon-specific nuclear gene fragments, and designed primers and probes that identified selected pollen taxa, even from routine aerobiological tape.
Preliminary quantification assays on pollen grains were successful in test species and mixes, with accuracy tested on 3 plant species.
However, the passages report feasibility and preliminary results rather than full operational validation for monitoring networks.
The evidence is partial: some aspects of prognosis can be predicted at disease onset, but relapse cannot be predicted.

In a prospective cohort of 176 patients with PMR followed for 5 years, elevated plasma viscosity (>=2.00 vs <=1.80 mPa s) and starting prednisolone >15 mg independently reduced the probability of stopping steroids within 5 years (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.29-0.82; HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41-0.97).

Late GCA was predicted on univariable analysis by female sex (OR 8.16), HLA-DRB1*0101 or -*0401 alleles (OR 4.95), elevated plasma viscosity (OR 10.64), and initial prednisolone >15 mg (OR 4.53), whereas no significant predictors of relapse were identified.

Yes—T-cell-deficient nude mice exposed to 90 ppm toluene showed longer escape latency than wild-type mice on acquisition days 3 and 4, suggesting T-cell deficiency can affect spatial learning after toluene exposure.

In 8-week-old male BALB/c mice, wild-type and nude mice were exposed to 0, 9, or 90 ppm toluene for 30 min/day for 3 consecutive days and then once weekly for 4 weeks before Morris water maze testing.

However, the effect of toluene on escape latency was not significant within nude mice, no significant reversal-phase differences were found, and only wild-type mice exposed to 90 ppm showed poor retention memory in the probe trial compared with controls.
Yes—patients in this study were overwhelmingly positive and willing participants in community-based medical education in regional and rural Australia.

In six rural and 11 regional New South Wales general practices in November 2008, 118 of 122 patients consented to medical student involvement, with 117 (99%) completing pre-consultation surveys and 100 (85%) completing post-consultation surveys.

Patients were positive about their doctor and practice being involved in student teaching and felt they played an important role, although before the consultation they were reluctant to let students conduct some or all of the consultation independently.
After the consultation, they reported they would have accepted higher levels of involvement than actually occurred.

No, prescriptions alone appear to be a poor proxy for asthma in children, especially in infants, because claims-based prescription criteria produced much higher prevalences and a different age pattern than survey-reported asthma. In 290,919 children aged 0-17 years in the GEK claims data, applying the prescription-based criteria of Stock et al. yielded asthma prevalences of 11.7-17.7% in boys and 7.2-11.1% in girls aged 0-4 years, with a steady decline in older age groups. In contrast, among 17,641 children aged 0-17 years in the KiGGS survey, prevalences in the same 0-4 year age group were only 0-2.6% in boys and 0-1.0% in girls, and prevalences increased with age after age 4.
No, IBS is not a diagnosis of exclusion; guidelines emphasize it should be positively diagnosed using the Rome criteria alone.

In a survey of nurse practitioners, primary care physicians, community gastroenterologists, and IBS experts, experts were less likely than nonexperts to endorse IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion (8% vs.
Experts were also more likely to make a positive diagnosis of IBS (67% vs.
38%, P<0.001), performed fewer tests (2.0 vs.
4.1, P<0.01), and spent less on testing ($297 vs. $658, P<0.01).
Providers who believed IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion ordered 1.6 more tests and spent $364 more (P<0.0001).

Yes, the training of ophthalmologist diplomates in West Africa can likely be improved, based on a survey of 2005 Trainee Ophthalmologist Diplomats that identified perceived problems and suggested changes.
The survey included 12 trainees (10 males, 2 females) in Ghana in 2006.
While 75.0% felt the programme was well structured and 66.7% felt allowances were adequate, 33.3% cited inadequate sponsorship, 33.3% cited short course duration, and 16.7% cited poor accommodation.
Suggested improvements included increasing training posts (33.3%), training allowance (25.0%), and incentives for trainers/training hospitals (16.7%).
No comparison group was reported, so these findings show trainee-perceived opportunities for improvement rather than tested interventions.

The evidence is mixed: in a proof-of-concept study, fenofibrate did not significantly reduce the apnoea/hypopnoea index but did improve some secondary sleep apnoea indices. In 34 subjects with mild to moderate sleep apnoea syndrome not treated with continuous positive airways pressure, randomized to fenofibrate 145 mg daily or placebo for 4 weeks, the AHI reduction versus control was 14% (95%CI -47 to 40%, p=0.533). However, fenofibrate significantly reduced the percentage of time with SpO2<90% (from 9.0% to 3.5% vs.
10.0% to 11.5% with placebo, p=0.007), reduced obstructive apnoeas by 44% (18.5 to 15.0 vs.
29.0 to 30.5, p=0.048), and reduced non-cortical micro-awakenings per hour (23.5 to 18.0 vs.
24.0 to 25.0, p=0.004). These exploratory findings are limited by short treatment duration and lack of correction for multiplicity.
The evidence is suggestive but does not directly establish that women residents delay childbearing due to perceived career threats.
In a survey of 424 residents (77% response), 41% of men versus 27% of women planned to have children during residency, and women had higher mean career-threat scores (2.9 vs 2.1, P =.001).
After adjustment, women were less likely to plan to have children during residency (odds ratio 0.46, 95% confidence interval 0.25-0.84), and threats to career explained 67% of the gender variance.
However, the outcome was intention to have children during residency, not actual delay, so the passages do not fully settle the delay question.

Yes, a limited opportunity for rescue antenatal corticosteroids exists, based on the finding that 124 of 692 women (17.9%) remained pregnant 1 week after antenatal corticosteroid administration and delivered before 34 weeks.
In a retrospective analysis of women at 24-32 weeks' gestation who received antenatal corticosteroids, 46.4% delivered within 1 week, including 13.3% within 24 hours.

Women who received antenatal corticosteroids for premature preterm rupture of membranes (OR 3.83, 95% CI 2.06-7.17), twins (OR 2.90, 95% CI 1.42-5.95), or before 28 weeks (OR 2.21, 95% CI 1.38-3.52) were more likely to deliver before 34 weeks.
The passage does not report whether rescue corticosteroids were actually given or their outcomes, but it identifies a subset remaining pregnant at 1 week who might be candidates for rescue.
Yes, in guinea pigs halofantrine caused cochlear damage at therapeutic and double therapeutic doses, but human evidence is absent.
In 30 guinea pigs divided into control, therapeutic-dose, and double-therapeutic-dose groups, control cochleae showed no changes.
The therapeutic dose caused loss and distortion of inner hair cells and inner phalangeal cells plus loss of spiral ganglia cells.
The double therapeutic dose distorted inner and outer hair cells and also caused loss of spiral ganglia cells.
The introduction notes that no studies have investigated halofantrine's effect on hearing in humans.

The evidence is insufficient to settle whether temperature should be routinely monitored during kidney allograft preservation. The study states that actual temperature conditions during cold storage are not known, so it monitored temperature with a probe in pig kidneys and human kidney grafts. Compared with the former storage can, the new can maintained the lowest temperature for 15 hours and stayed below 5°C for 57 hours, whereas the former can maintained the lowest temperature for 80 minutes and reached 5°C after 10 hours 40 minutes. Temperature levels were similar regardless of probe position and with 2 vs 4 kg of crushed ice, and similar results were observed in human grafts. Thus, monitoring can reveal differences in preservation conditions, but the passages do not provide a recommendation on routine clinical use.

Yes, leptin appears to be involved in phagocytic NADPH oxidase overactivity in obesity, based on a positive correlation and in vitro induction. In 164 obese and 94 normal-weight controls, phagocytic NADPH oxidase activity and plasma leptin were both higher in obese patients (P<0.05), and NADPH oxidase activity positively correlated with leptin in obese patients, remaining significant in multivariate analysis. The evidence is mixed: in one series, kidneys from donors older than 60 implanted into recipients younger than 60 had similar 10-year patient and graft survival compared with younger donor-recipient pairs, but significantly worse renal function.
The study included 91 consecutive transplants from cadaver donors older than 60 into recipients younger than 60, compared with 91 matched controls with donors and recipients younger than 60.
At 1, 5, and 10 years, patient survival was 97.6%, 87.2%, and 76.6% vs.
93.9%, 76.4%, and 69.5% (P=0.980), and death-censored graft survival was 94.4%, 92.6%, and 77.4% vs.
