Medial PTS ≥5° had an odds ratio of 6.8 for ACLR failure (P = 0.007), and lateral PTS ≥5° had an odds ratio of 10.8 (P = 0.000).
These findings support an association, but they come from a single small retrospective study and do not by themselves prove causation.

The evidence is mixed: in a trial of feedback after weight screening, 94% of parents of overweight children correctly recalled their child's weight status, but fewer than 10 parents could accurately describe what the measurements meant.

Among 271 overweight children aged 4–8 years, 244 (90%) parents completed a 2-week follow-up; overall they recalled 39% of the information (mean 6.3 of 16), and parents given best-practice-care feedback recalled slightly more than those given motivational interviewing (difference 0.48; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.92).
Thus the passages show good recall of the weight-status label but poor understanding of its meaning, with maternal education and perceived usefulness predicting recall scores.
The evidence is mixed: the passages support that sternal fractures are rare in growing children but do not address whether they are often overlooked.
In a 2-year period from January 2010 to December 2012, all inpatients and outpatients with sternal fractures were recorded, and only 4 children aged 5–14 years were treated.
Of these, 2 children were hospitalized for pain management and 2 remained in outpatient care.
The background states that sternal fractures in childhood are rare , but no supplied passage reports diagnostic delay or missed detection to substantiate the “often overlooked” claim.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that government assistance improves eye care utilization by low-income individuals; the study found lower utilization among those with financial difficulty despite assistance programs.

Among 27,375 white Canadian Community Health Survey respondents, middle-aged whites without glaucoma, cataracts, diabetes, or uncorrected vision problems had eye care utilization of 28.1% if they had financial difficulty versus 41.9% if they did not (p<0.05; adjusted prevalence ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.57-0.80).

The study also showed that low-income vision care assistance fully covered a general/routine eye examination in only 5 provinces, was insufficient in the remainder, and eyeglasses assistance was inadequate in 5 provinces, requiring out-of-pocket copayments.

In that prospective pilot study, 23 consecutive patients (12 male, 11 female) with stage III or stages III and IV OCD lesions admitted for surgery had serum vitamin D3 measured, and their mean age was 31.3 years.

The study aimed to analyze whether vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency might be a contributing etiological factor, but these descriptive findings alone do not settle whether it is related to development.
No, timing of initial surfactant treatment did not appear to make a difference in rates of chronic lung disease or mortality in premature infants after multivariable analysis.

In a retrospective analysis of 2170 premature infants born at 22–32 weeks' gestation in 10 Australian NICUs, 1182 received early surfactant (within one hour of birth) and 988 received late surfactant.
Although the early group was less mature (27.1 vs 29.4 weeks) and had higher unadjusted CLD/mortality (40.2% vs 20.0%), the multivariable analysis showed little or no impact on CLD/mortality.

Yes, the evidence supports the inverse equity hypothesis in these middle-income countries: economic inequalities in cancer screening participation were substantially lower or non-existent in countries with higher aggregate coverage.

In cross-sectional WHO SAGE data from China, Mexico, Russia, and South Africa (2007–2010), breast cancer screening coverage ranged from 10.5% in South Africa to 43% in Mexico, and cervical cancer screening coverage ranged from 24% in South Africa to 81.5% in Russia.

The relative index of inequality for breast screening was 14.57 in South Africa versus 1.04 in Russia, and for cervical screening was 3.60 in China versus 1.12 in Russia, showing narrower inequalities at higher coverage.
Yes, but the evidence is mixed: some circulating androgens correlate with sexual desire in women, while the overall correlation is described as inconclusive.
In a cross-sectional study of 560 healthy women aged 19-65, sexual desire on the Female Sexual Function Index correlated overall with free testosterone and androstenedione.

In women aged 25-44 not using systemic hormonal contraception, desire correlated with total testosterone, free testosterone, androstenedione, and DHEAS, while in women aged 45-65 only androstenedione correlated.
The androgen metabolite ADT-G did not correlate with sexual desire.

The evidence is insufficient to say whether participant information sheet content and presentation influence actual recruitment or participation in an antenatal intervention, because the supplied study measured only perceptions, not recruitment or participation.

In that study, 35 pregnant women and 36 trainee midwives were randomized to four information sheets differing in title and font fluency (Double Fluent, Double Awkward, Fluent Title–Awkward Font, Awkward Title–Fluent Font) and rated the intervention on five-point Likert scales for attractiveness, complexity, expected risk, and required effort.
The only reported significant result was that pregnant women rated the Double Awkward sheet as more complex than the Double Fluent sheet (p=.024) and the Awkward Title–Fluent Font sheet (p=.021).
Thus the passages show a processing-fluency effect on perceived complexity but do not show effects on recruitment or participation.
The evidence is mixed: upper airway surgery significantly lowered some serum lipids but not others in obstructive sleep apnea patients.

In a retrospective review of 113 adults with OSA who underwent nasal or uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) surgery, serum total cholesterol decreased from 4.86±0.74 to 4.69±0.71 and lipoprotein(a) decreased from a median of 18.50 to 10.90 (P<0.01 and 0.01, respectively), while HDL, LDL, and triglycerides showed no significant changes (P>0.05 for all).
Subgroup results varied: UPPP patients (n=51) improved in total cholesterol, HDL, and lipoprotein(a), whereas nasal surgery patients (n=62) only had a decrease in lipoprotein(a).

The evidence is mixed: in a population-based cohort of 1,100 randomly sampled Saskatchewan adults, increasing neck pain severity was associated with worse physical health-related quality of life (HRQoL) 6 months later, but not with mental HRQoL.

Compared with participants without neck pain at baseline, those with mild (β=-1.53, 95% CI -2.83 to -0.24), intense (β=-3.60, 95% CI -5.76 to -1.44), or disabling (β=-8.55, 95% CI -11.68 to -5.42) neck pain had worse physical HRQoL at 6 months after adjustment.
A worsening or persistent course of neck pain was also associated with worse physical HRQoL, while no association was found between neck pain and mental HRQoL.

The evidence is insufficient to definitively establish that bone thickness and inter-radicular space affect miniscrew placement, but the study reports these as primary outcome variables in the posterior mandible.

In 100 patients (mean age 17.4 ± 6.74 years; 61 female, 39 male; 60 Class I and 40 Class II molar relationships), inter-radicular space ranged from 2.46 to 3.31 mm and alveolar bone thickness ranged from 8.01 to 13.77 mm, with thickness decreasing as insertion angle increased from 45° to 90°.
No significant differences were found between genders or malocclusion types.
The passages do not report miniscrew placement success or failure, so they do not directly demonstrate an effect on placement.
No—most elderly patients in this study did not correctly endorse calling 911 for stroke scenarios.
Among 367 out-patients aged ≥60 in Buenos Aires, only 14% correctly endorsed intention to call 911 on the Stroke Action Test using a ≥75% cutoff.
For the most typical stroke signs and symptoms, only 65% reported they would call an ambulance, and the correct response was chosen only 37% of the time on average.
This reflects intended rather than actual 911 calling, and higher education was associated with better endorsement.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) can differentiate unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS) from minimally conscious state (MCS).

In 25 severe disorders of consciousness patients and 20 healthy controls, baseline electrophysiological evaluation showed partial preservation of cortical effective connectivity and excitability in clinically defined MCS but absence in clinically defined UWS.

However, anodal tDCS over the orbitofrontal cortex boosted cortical connectivity and excitability in all healthy controls and MCS patients and unmasked such excitability/connectivity in some UWS patients.

Thus, the supplied passages show baseline measures differentiated MCS from UWS, but they do not show that tDCS itself reliably separates the groups and even suggest tDCS may unmask residual connectivity in some UWS.
Yes—plate clearing tendencies were positively associated with BMI in a US adult cohort, supporting plate clearing as a risk factor for obesity.

In 993 US adults (60% male, 80% American European, mean age 31), greater self-reported habitual plate clearing was associated with higher BMI (β=0.18, 95% CI 0.07–0.29, P<0.001) after accounting for demographic and behavioral predictors.
The study is observational and shows association, not causation, so it does not by itself prove that plate clearing causes obesity.
The evidence is mixed but suggests MRI may have a limited adjunctive or alternative role to MDCT, though it does not replace EUS for sensitivity.
In a prospective study of 52 patients, MRI had T-staging sensitivity 76% and specificity 89%, compared with MDCT (65% sensitivity, 91% specificity) and EUS (94% sensitivity, 60% specificity).
For N staging, MRI sensitivity was 69% and specificity 73%, versus MDCT (73% sensitivity, 81% specificity) and EUS (92% sensitivity, 58% specificity).
Adding MRI to MDCT or EUS did not significantly improve sensitivity, so its incremental value remains unclear.

Yes, distal ureteral diameter (UD) predicted reflux resolution after endoscopic injection in a retrospective review of children with primary vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). The study included 70 patients (17 boys and 53 girls; mean age 5.9 years), with grade III VUR in 53% and grade IV in 47%, all treated with Macroplastique injection. Both distal UD and UD ratio were significant predictors of reflux resolution on logistic regression analysis (P <.007 and P =.001, respectively).

Yes—loss of DKK3 expression was associated with lymph node metastasis and, when combined with CT, improved the accuracy of CT staging for predicting lymph node involvement from 71.5% to 80.0% in advanced gastric cancer.
This rests on 158 gastric cancer patients who underwent gastrectomy, in whom DKK3 loss occurred in 64/158 (40.5%) and was associated with lymph node metastasis (p<0.001).
The passage reports the combined prediction in advanced gastric cancer patients using preoperative CT stage, but it does not specify whether DKK3 itself was measured preoperatively.
Yes—the Transmissible Liability Index (TLI) assessed at age 10–12 predicted later suicidal behavior, including number and severity of lifetime suicide attempts.

In a longitudinal study of 500 males, 250 sons of men with lifetime substance use disorder (High Average Risk) and 250 sons of men without lifetime substance use disorder (Low Average Risk), TLI was measured at baseline and with age-specific versions at ages 12–14, 16, 19, 22, and 25.
TLI was significantly associated with number and severity of lifetime suicide attempts across follow-up into young adulthood.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that gingival crevicular blood can be relied upon for assessing blood glucose levels, because the supplied study only reports a very strong correlation with finger-prick blood rather than agreement or diagnostic accuracy.
In 75 patients with chronic periodontitis (43 males, 32 females), blood oozing from gingival crevices after periodontal probing was compared with finger-prick blood glucose measurements.
Patient glucose values ranged from 74 to 256 mg/dl, and the comparison showed a very strong correlation (t = 3.97, P = 0.001).
Thus, the study supports a strong association but does not establish that gingival crevicular blood is reliable for clinical assessment.

The evidence is insufficient to say clinical supervision can sustain the workforce in the current healthcare landscape, because the supplied study measured perceived effectiveness rather than workforce sustainability.

It surveyed community allied health workers (n = 82) 8 months after structured clinical supervision and found that session length (r(s) ≥ 0.44), number of sessions (r(s) ≥ 0.35), and total period of supervision (r(s) ≥ 0.42) were positively correlated with MCSS-26 effectiveness domains, while receiving supervision, having choice of supervisor, and having a completed supervision agreement were associated with higher total MCSS-26 scores (P(s) < 0.014).
However, the passages do not report retention, turnover, or intention-to-stay outcomes, so they do not show whether clinical supervision sustains the workforce.
The evidence is insufficient to settle whether high-IQ schizophrenia is a clinically distinct sub-type; it shows distinct symptom features but does not establish full subtype validity.

In 29 schizophrenia patients with exceptionally high pre-morbid intelligence (mean estimated IQ 120), about half also had minimal post-onset IQ decline (<10 points), and they were compared with schizophrenia patients of typical IQ using multinomial logistic regression.

High-IQ patients had significantly lower negative and disorganised symptoms than typical patients (RRR=0.019; 95% CI=0.001–0.675, P=0.030) and better global functioning and insight (RRR=1.082; 95% CI=1.020–1.148; P=0.009).
Those with minimal post-onset IQ decline also showed higher manic symptoms (RRR=8.213; 95% CI=1.042–64.750, P=0.046).

No, the probability of prenatal diagnosis or termination of pregnancy for fetal anomaly was not statistically different between fetuses with congenital heart defects conceived by assisted reproductive techniques (ART) and those conceived spontaneously.

In a population-based Paris study, prenatal diagnosis was 28.1% in ART-conceived (n=171) versus 34.6% in spontaneously conceived (n=4620) fetuses (P=0.077), and termination for fetal anomaly was 36.2% versus 39.2% (P=0.677).
Adjusted estimates were similar, and gestational age at termination was comparable.
This finding is limited to congenital heart defects, not all congenital anomalies.

Yes, emergency physicians can accurately and reliably assess acute vertigo using the STANDING tool, based on high sensitivity and specificity for central acute vertigo and good inter-observer agreement.

In a prospective study of 98 adult patients with isolated vertigo in a single academic ED, five trained emergency physicians with limited nystagmus experience used STANDING, compared with senior audiologist evaluation corroborated by neuroimaging as the reference standard.

They found sensitivity 92.9% (95% CI 70-100%) and specificity 96.4% (95% CI 93-38%) for central acute vertigo, with 13 true positives, 3 false positives, 81 true negatives, and 1 false negative; the whole test had good inter-observer agreement (k = 0.76, 95% CI 0.45-1).

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that this is a validated improvement to NF EN 13727; the authors only suggest trial conditions adapted from that standard because no standard protocol existed for skin/mucosal antiseptics with interfering substances.

They tested three solutions—chlorhexidine-benzalkonium (CB), hexamidine-chlorhexidine-chlorocresol (HCC), and povidone iodine (P)—on recommended strains at 97%, 50%, 10%, and 1%, expecting a ≥5 log reduction after 60 seconds.

CB had the most homogeneous bactericidal activity, with >5 log reduction on all 4 bacterial strains at 97%, 50%, and 10%; HCC showed no bactericidal activity except against P. aeruginosa at 97%, and P was not bactericidal against E. hirae at any concentration or S. aureus at 97%.
Thus, the passages show proposed adapted conditions and comparative activity results, not a proven improvement over the standard.
The evidence is mixed: Web-based and clinic samples of gay men living with HIV differed on psychological symptom burden but not on physical symptom burden.
The comparison included 154 London-resident gay men recruited from a UK-wide Web survey and 400 gay men recruited from five London HIV outpatient clinics.

The Web sample had worse mean psychological symptom burden than the clinic sample (1.61, SD 1.09 vs 1.36, SD 0.96), and in multivariable analysis adjusted for age, ethnicity, employment status, and ART use, Web recruitment was associated with being in the worst psychological symptom tertile (adjusted OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.41-3.44, P=.001).
Physical symptom burden means were similar (0.78, SD 0.65 vs 0.70, SD 0.74), and recruitment setting was not significantly associated with high physical symptom score in the adjusted model.
Yes, sensation returns to the nasal tip after microfat injections; in a prospective study of 30 young women, touch threshold recovered gradually and paresthesia diminished to none.
The population was 30 young women (age 20.04 ± 3.63 years) at Beijing Anzhen Hospital, and the comparison was nasal tip sensation over time after microfat injections.

Mean touch threshold was 3.60 units preoperatively, decreased by 2.50 units at week 1, then recovered to 1.51 units at week 2, 2.39 units at week 4, 3.01 units at week 8, and 3.35 units at week 12, with significant differences between measurement points (P<.05).

Yes, this single-center retrospective series supports that minimally invasive mitral valve repair with artificial chords is reproducible and applicable in routine surgery, with a 99.8% repair rate and no reoperations during follow-up. In 426 consecutive patients (mean age 55 ± 18 years) undergoing video-assisted mitral valve repair from 2008 to 2013, neochords were used in all patients, with leaflet resection in 47. The study was a single-arm review with no comparator group; postoperatively 15 patients (3.5%) had Grade I regurgitation and the remainder had none, and at 3-60 months all patients had no or trace mitral regurgitation, with no neochord de-insertion or rupture and no reoperations. The authors explicitly aimed to assess the effectiveness and reproducibility of neochordal repair as a routine approach.
Yes, emergency general surgery laparotomies are associated with high 30-day and 1-year mortality, particularly in older patients, indicating an area of concern and need for improvement.

In a retrospective study of 477 laparotomies in 446 patients, 30-day mortality was 12.4% in those aged <70 years and 22% in those aged >70 years (p<0.001), while 1-year mortality was 25.15% in those aged <70 years and 38% in those aged >70 years (p<0.001).
The authors aimed to analyse these outcomes to encourage prospective data collection and improvement of care.
Yes, certain preresidency selection criteria predict some measures of performance in orthopaedic surgery residency, based on a study of 60 residents from one institution.

Objective performance showed moderate correlations between ABOS Part I scores and USMLE Step 2 scores (r = 0.55, p < 0.001) and number of clinical honors (r = 0.45, p < 0.001), while OITE scores had weak correlations with clinical honors (r = 0.35, p = 0.009) and USMLE Step 2 (r = 0.29, p = 0.02).

Subjectively, Alpha Omega Alpha membership was associated with higher global evaluation scores (p = 0.005), with a correlation of r = 0.60 (p = 0.005), strongest for interpersonal and communication skills.
The passages do not report predictive value for all listed criteria, such as MCAT scores, letters of recommendation, away rotations, or publications.
Yes, zero CLABSI rate was sustainable in this NICU, with the rate maintained at zero for >600 days after interventions.

In a NICU at the Floating Hospital for Children at Tufts Medical Center, adoption of standardized care practices including bundles and checklists was associated with a reduction to zero CLABSI for >370 consecutive days in 2012.

After a brief increase to 3.3 per 1000 line days in the first quarter of 2013, a series of interventions maintained the CLABSI rate at zero for >600 days, with overall rates falling from 4.1 per 1000 line days in 2009 to 0.94 in 2013 (77% reduction).
Ongoing training, surveillance, vigilance with catheter practices, and improved documentation were identified as key drivers.
However, this is a single-center experience, so the passages do not establish sustainability in other settings.

The evidence is mixed/insufficient: the study found no association between arch form and significant Bolton tooth-size discrepancy, but it did not report whether arch form is associated with sagittal molar relationship.
In 230 Saudi orthodontic patients, mandibular casts were classified as tapered, ovoid, or square, and Bolton ratio and Angle classification were analyzed.
No association was observed between significant Bolton discrepancy and arch form or sagittal molar relationship.
Thus, Bolton discrepancy does not appear to influence arch form, while the influence of sagittal molar relationship remains unaddressed by these results.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that outcome feedback in emergency medicine training is an opportunity to apply deliberate practice theory, because the supplied study does not assess deliberate practice.

It shows that mandatory active outcome feedback was absent in all surveyed Canadian Royal College EM programs for admitted or discharged patients (0/21), while follow-up was elective for 89.4% of residents for admitted patients and 44.2% for discharged patients.

Residents more often than program directors believed follow-up should be mandatory (76.9% vs 42.9%, p=0.002) and rated outcome feedback’s educational value higher (5.8/7 vs 5.1/7, difference 0.7, p=0.002).
Thus, the passages show a gap in mandatory outcome feedback and high resident-perceived value, but they do not directly show whether this is an opportunity to apply deliberate practice theory.

No, luteal estradiol + GnRH antagonist pretreatment before microdose leuprolide did not improve IVF outcomes in poor responders compared with oral contraceptive pill pretreatment, and the OCP group actually had a significantly higher ongoing pregnancy rate.
This retrospective study included 130 poor responders undergoing IVF with either OCP/ML or E2+antag/ML protocols.
Ongoing pregnancy rates were 40% vs 15% in favor of OCP/ML, with no significant differences in gonadotropin requirement, cancellation rate, or number of embryos transferred.
Trends toward more oocytes retrieved (7.7 ± 3.4 vs.
5.9 ± 4.2) and improved implantation (20% vs.
12%) also favored OCP/ML but were not statistically significant.

Yes; an observational study of 431 dental patients found sublingual varices were associated with hypertension (OR = 2.25, p<0.002). In that study, patients with grade 1 (medium/severe) sublingual varices had higher mean systolic (132 vs 123 mmHg) and diastolic (83 vs 80 mmHg) blood pressure than those with grade 0 (none/few). The same study reported a positive predictive value of 0.5 and a negative predictive value of 0.80 for sublingual varices indicating hypertension. As an observational clinical study, this supports an association but not causation.
Yes, the clinical presentation of a prior spontaneous preterm birth predicts risk in a subsequent pregnancy.

In a retrospective cohort of 522 singleton pregnancies with prior spontaneous preterm birth, recurrent preterm birth occurred in 55.2% of those with prior advanced cervical dilatation versus 27.2% with prior preterm premature rupture of membranes and 32.2% with prior preterm labor (P =.001).

Mean gestational age at delivery was also lower after prior advanced cervical dilatation (34.0 weeks) than after prior preterm premature rupture of membranes (37.2 weeks) or prior preterm labor (37.0 weeks), and the lowest mean cervical length before 24 weeks was shorter in the advanced cervical dilatation group.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that biofeedback training enhances athletes' sport performance.
In highly competent athletes aged 16–34, 18 experimental athletes (4 women, 14 men) received biofeedback training while 21 controls (4 women, 17 men) did not, with stress tests before and after.

The experimental group showed greater psychophysiological control, with significant results for GSR regulation (p=0.037), HR after the STROOP stressor (p=0.037), GSR after the math stressor (p=0.033), and HR-breathing coherence after the math stressor (p=0.042).
However, the passages report no measured athletic-performance outcome; the only performance-related follow-up was a one-year questionnaire asking whether athletes perceived subsequent enhancement.
No—unenhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted MRI did not reliably differentiate bone infarcts from acute osteomyelitis in children with sickle cell disease.

In a retrospective review of 31 children with SCD and acute bone pain (20 boys, 11 girls; mean age 10.6 years), 5 were classified as positive for osteomyelitis and 26 as positive for bone infarct by clinical standard.
Bone marrow signal intensity on T1-W fat-saturated imaging was not significant for differentiation (P = 0.56), and no additional evaluated unenhanced MRI parameters proved reliable.
Likely yes: the lifetime model gave an ICER of £482/QALY, below the £30,000/QALY willingness-to-pay threshold, though probabilistic sensitivity analysis showed uncertainty.
This was based on 612 pregnant women in Glasgow randomized to usual cessation support plus or minus up to £400 in vouchers, comparing cotinine-validated quitters, QALYs, and NHS costs.
The incremental cost per quitter at 34–38 weeks was £1127, and the lifetime model found an incremental cost of £17 and a gain of 0.04 QALYs.
The evidence therefore supports cost-effectiveness, but uncertainty—particularly about relapse after birth—means additional research may be worthwhile.
The evidence is mixed: nurse-led preoperative education reduced anxiety in cardiac surgery patients, but its effect on postoperative complications is not clearly established.

In a randomized trial of 395 elective cardiac surgery patients, the intervention group (n=205) received preoperative education by trained nurses while controls (n=190) received standard ward information.
State anxiety on the day before surgery decreased only in the intervention group (34.0 vs 36.9, P=0.001), and the mean state-anxiety decrease was greater in the intervention group (P=0.001).

No significant difference was found in length of stay or readmission, and the reported chest infection result was lower in the intervention group (10 (5.3%) vs 1 (0.5%), P=0.004), although those numbers appear inconsistent with the stated direction.
Yes, but detection is partial: rapid prescreening (RPS) flagged 39 of 107 (36.4%) Pap smears with a final interpretation of glandular cell abnormality (≥AGC).
That finding comes from 80,565 Pap smears that underwent RPS over 25 months, where samples were designated "review for abnormality" if abnormal cells at the AGC threshold were thought present.
RPS also uniquely picked up 11 AGC cases not detected by full screening, 2 of which had endometrial adenocarcinoma on follow-up.
Thus, the evidence shows RPS detects some glandular cell abnormalities, but it does not detect most, and no prior study had specifically assessed RPS sensitivity for glandular abnormalities.

Yes, pelvic anatomical structures are at risk during arthroscopic acetabular labral repair when drilling is not depth-controlled, as a cadaveric study found injuries only with free drill penetrations.
In ten cadaveric hips, free drill penetrations caused 14 injuries in 60 penetrations (23.3%), whereas no injuries occurred with stopped drill penetrations.
The risk of perforation into the pelvic cavity began at 20 mm drill depth, and the mean bone depth across insertions was 31.7 mm (SD 2.6).
Yes, for diminutive polyps, a cut and discard approach using optical diagnosis could ease the financial burden by saving $319.77 per patient.

In a prospective cohort of 94 patients with 159 diminutive (≤5 mm) polyps, optical diagnosis was correct in 105/108 adenomas (97.2%) and correctly triaged 92 (98%) patients to surveillance colonoscopy.
Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were 97.2%, 78.4%, 90.5%, and 93%, respectively, against histological assessment.
However, these findings are limited to diminutive polyps and do not show whether the broader financial burden of colonoscopy can be eased.

The evidence is mixed: in octogenarians undergoing cardiac reoperation, in-hospital mortality was 32.1% and another 19.0% died during follow-up, yet survivors had good functional status and quality of life comparable to an age- and sex-matched normative population.

This comes from 84 consecutive patients aged ≥80 years who underwent cardiac reoperation between 2007 and 2013, with mean age 81.9 ± 1.9 years, and no nonoperative or alternative-treatment comparison group was reported.

Among survivors, mean Barthel Index was 89 ± 17, mean NYHA class was 2 ± 1, 93% were living at home, and SF-12 physical and mental summary scores equalled an age- and sex-matched normative population.

Thus the passages show substantial early mortality but favorable survivor status, and without a comparison group they do not establish whether reoperation itself confers a net benefit over alternatives.

No, mammographic density did not have an independent impact on margin re-excision rates after breast-conserving surgery in this study, as the bivariable trend toward more re-excision in denser breasts disappeared in multivariable analysis.
Among 655 women with breast cancer, 398 (60.8%) underwent breast-conserving surgery, and 166 (41.7%) of those required separate re-excision.

Patients with denser breasts by BI-RADS and volumetric density showed a trend toward more frequent re-excision in bivariable analysis, but this association was not seen in multivariable analysis, and the rate of unnecessary margins did not differ by breast density.
In multivariable analysis, re-excision rates increased with DCIS and decreased with resection of additional margins, not with mammographic density.
Yes, evidence from a natural experiment in an internal medicine service indicates that evidence-based practice improved some patient outcomes.
Following reorganization into an EBP unit, EBP patients had lower mortality than standard-practice patients (6.27% vs 7.75%, P<0.001) and shorter length of stay (6.01 vs 8.46 days, P<0.001).
The EBP doctors' own mortality dropped from 7.4% to 6.3% (P<0.02) and length of stay from 9.15 to 6.01 days (P=0.002), with no statistically significant improvements in standard practice.
Readmission rates were similar (14.4% EBP vs 14.5% SP).

No, the study did not show additional value of sst2a IHC over SRS uptake: among 73 GEP-NET patients selected for PRRT based on positive SRS, 93% were sst2a IHC-positive but IHC status was not significantly related to best GEP-NET response 1 year after PRRT (p = 0.47).
The analysis compared in vitro sst2a IHC with in vivo response, and the background explicitly stated it was unknown whether IHC has additional value compared with SRS uptake.
Thus, these passages do not demonstrate added predictive value for sst2a IHC beyond SRS uptake.
No, the study found no response to load in either T1DM or control group over the 4 days post exercise.
It compared 7 individuals with T1DM and 10 controls who regularly ran >5 km; baseline tendon structure was similar (UTC echo-types I-IV and anterior-posterior thickness all p > 0.05).
Thus, in this small comparison, T1DM did not affect Achilles tendon response to a 10 km run.

Yes—teleoncology-supervised chemotherapy in Mount Isa produced no significant differences from the tertiary centre in dose intensity, side effects, or hospital admissions, and there were no toxicity-related deaths in either group.

In a quasi-experimental comparison, 89 rural patients received 626 chemotherapy cycles in Mount Isa under teleoncology supervision by the same medical oncologists, while 117 comparison patients received 799 cycles at Townsville Cancer Centre.
The two groups showed no significant differences in most demographic characteristics, mean treatment cycles, dose intensities, proportions of side effects, or hospital admissions.
Yes—baseline PRO data captured by FTE-dependent versus non-FTE-dependent methods were highly correlated and not significantly different.
In 119 adults who underwent 1- and 2-level lumbar fusions at Duke, patients completed phone-interview and self-survey questionnaires for ODI, VAS-BP, and VAS-LP.

Correlations were ODI r=-0.89, VAS-BP r=0.74, and VAS-LP r=0.70, and baseline means did not differ (ODI 47.73±16.77 vs 45.81±12.11, P=0.39; VAS-LP 6.13±2.78 vs 6.46±2.79, P=0.36; VAS-BP 6.33±2.90 vs 6.53±2.48, P=0.57).
Preliminary evidence suggests yes: intravenous opioid patient-controlled therapy (PCT) reduced refractory breathlessness in advanced disease, though this comes from a small pilot observational study.

In 18 inpatients with advanced cancer and refractory breathlessness (median age 57.5 years; 77.8% female), self-reported current breathlessness on a numeric rating scale decreased from a baseline median of 5 (range 1-10) to 4 on Day 1 (range 0-8, P < 0.01) and 4 on Day 2 (range 0-5, P < 0.01), with stable physiological parameters.
Daily morphine equivalent dose was median 20.3 mg on Day 1, 13.0 mg on Day 2, and 16.0 mg on Day 3, and on Day 3, 12/12 patients confirmed that this mode of application provided relief.
However, because this was a pilot observational study with 18 patients, it supports feasibility and acceptance but does not definitively establish opioid PCT as a new standard therapeutic concept.
Yes, viral infections appear to have a role in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) based on higher serologic values for most studied viruses in BPPV patients.

In a retrospective study, 483 patients with BPPV were compared with 461 healthy controls, and serologic analysis was performed for HSV1, HSV2, herpes zoster, EBV, CMV, adenovirus, influenza, and parainfluenza virus.
All viral serology values except influenza and parainfluenza were higher in the BPPV group than in the control group, and seasonal variations were observed.
The study was retrospective.
The evidence is mixed: some surrogates of injury severity influence the occurrence of heterotopic ossification, but the injury severity score itself does not.

In a retrospective review of 241 patients treated with a posterior approach for acetabular fractures, ICU length of stay (1-2 days OR 4.33, 95% CI 1.03-18.25; 3-6 days OR 4.1, 95% CI 1.27-13.27; >6 days OR 11.7, 95% CI 3.24-42.22) and non-ICU length of stay >10 days (OR 7.6, 95% CI 2.6-22.25) were significantly associated with HO development in multivariate modeling.
However, injury severity score, mechanism of injury, presence of neurologic injury, and other factors were not significantly associated with HO development or severity.
XRT HO prophylaxis was associated with reduced odds (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.10-0.85).

Yes, less invasive management appears safe and effective for a contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion, based on no subsequent hydrocele or hernia after scrotal-only treatment. In a review of 37 neonates with torsion, 22 had a contralateral hydrocele at presentation, and all hydroceles were opened through a scrotal approach at the time of contralateral scrotal fixation without inguinal exploration. After an average 7.5-year follow-up (range 4.3-11.2 years), none of these patients developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia. The passages support that avoiding an inguinal incision to minimize spermatic cord injury did not lead to later hydrocele or hernia, though they do not directly compare this approach with inguinal repair.
The evidence is mixed: PIBS dose-point evaluation was reproducible in this small study, but it did not capture all significant vaginal dose variation.

In 19 patients who received image-guided brachytherapy after concurrent radiochemotherapy, delivered doses at PIBS -2, PIBS, and PIBS +2 were compared with prescribed doses, and applicator movement relative to the PIBS point was analyzed.

Mean prescribed doses at PIBS -2, PIBS, and PIBS +2 were 2.23 ± 1.4, 6.39 ± 6.6, and 31.85 ± 36.06 Gy; delivered doses at the four points were strongly correlated with prescribed doses (R² 0.93–0.95), and variations at PIBS points were not significant.

However, the 5 patients with vaginal involvement had significantly higher doses than the 14 without at PIBS +2 (+47.60 Gy, p=0.023) and PIBS (+7.46 Gy, p=0.03), and delivered dose at the ICRU rectovaginal point was 1.43 ± 2.49 Gy lower than planned (p=0.019).
Thus, these passages support partial reliability of PIBS dose-point reporting but do not settle whether dose-point evaluation alone is sufficient for vaginal dose assessment.
The evidence is mixed: young-onset colorectal cancer shows significant clinicopathological differences from older-onset disease, but overall survival is similar.

In a retrospective cohort of 330 patients, those diagnosed at age ≤40 years were matched 1:2 with patients >50 years and had higher rates of family history (p=0.003), hereditary syndromes (p<0.0001), IBD (p=0.007), lower polyps (p<0.0001), and more stage III/IV disease (p=0.001), angiolymphatic invasion, signet ring adenocarcinoma, and rectal tumors (p=0.02).
Younger patients had worse 5-year disease-free survival (57.6 vs 70%, p=0.039), but this lost significance by stage (p=0.092), and 5-year overall survival was similar (59.1 vs 62.1%, p=0.565).
Thus it may be a distinct clinical entity based on presentation and pathology, but not on overall survival.
Yes, adjustment for reporting heterogeneity appears necessary in sleep disorders because it changed the factors found to be significantly associated with sleep-related problems.

In 1002 Japanese adults aged 18 years and over, without correction age, sex, and number of comorbidities were significantly associated with greater severity of sleep-related problems, but after correction sex was no longer significant and regular exercise became significant.

The Compound Hierarchical Ordered Probit model with anchoring vignettes produced these changes compared with the ordered probit model, although the difference in the magnitude of regression coefficients was subtle.
Thus the passages show that adjustment can alter substantive conclusions about sleep disorder correlates, supporting the need for it.

Overall, nurses were not better than the simple objective GAPS score for predicting admission at triage; GAPS and nurses' VAS had comparable discrimination (AUC 0.876 vs 0.875, p=0.93) and binary accuracy (80.6% vs 79.0%, p=0.18), while nurses overestimated admissions (47.3% vs observed 40.7%, p<0.0001).

In the majority of attendances where nurses were less than 95% certain, GAPS significantly outperformed nurses on calibration (+1.2% vs +9.2%, p<0.0001), discrimination (AUC 0.810 vs 0.759, p=0.001), and accuracy (75.1% vs 68.9%, p=0.0009).

When nurses felt at least 95% certain, their VAS accuracy was excellent at 92.4%, and a strategy using GAPS but over-ruling it with ≥95% clinical certainty outperformed either method alone (AUC 0.891, accuracy 82.5%).
Yes, the evidence indicates that depression diagnosis and antidepressant prescribing vary by neighbourhood ethnic density, though the pattern differs by ethnic group.

In a study of just over one million GP patients in Lambeth, Hackney, Tower Hamlets, and Newham in 2013, a 10% increase in own-ethnic density was associated with lower odds of new depression diagnosis for Pakistani (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70-0.93), Indian (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81-0.95), African (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.78-0.99), and Bangladeshi (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.90-0.99) patients, but higher odds for Black Caribbean patients (OR 1.26, 95% CI 1.09-1.46).
Antidepressant prescribing showed very similar results, although the Black Caribbean association was no longer statistically significant (p=0.07).
The passages do not directly compare variation across the four boroughs; they show variation by neighbourhood ethnic density within the study area.
Yes—duplex Doppler ultrasonography can non-invasively diagnose esophageal varices in compensated hepatic cirrhosis, resting on the splenoportal index (SPI).
In 56 patients with compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A), SPI was predictive of varices, and at a cut-off of 5.0 it had 88% diagnostic accuracy using endoscopy as the reference standard.

For SPI <5.0, absence of varices was correctly diagnosed in 27 of 28 patients (negative predictive value 96%, sensitivity 96%), while for SPI ≥5.0, presence was correctly diagnosed in 22 of 28 (positive predictive value 79%, specificity 82%).
Other indices (HARI, HAPI, SARI, SAPI) were not helpful (p > 0.05).

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that the novel vascular-guided multilayer preauricular approach (VMPA) improves access and reduces complications compared with other approaches, because the study had no comparison group.

In a retrospective consecutive series of patients without prior TMJ surgery who underwent TMJ surgery via VMPA in 2013 and were followed at least 6 months, all 606 joints had successful surgeries and all incisions healed favorably with uneventful recovery.
No patient developed permanent facial nerve weakness or other severe complications.
The study was designed to investigate whether VMPA could improve access and decrease complications, but without a comparator it does not establish improvement or reduction.

No—among high bleeding risk (HBR) patients undergoing PCI, bare-metal stent (BMS) implantation was associated with worse 12-month outcomes than the zotarolimus-eluting Endeavor Sprint stent (E-ZES) when both were followed by 30-day dual antiplatelet therapy.

In the ZEUS trial, 828 HBR patients were randomized to E-ZES or BMS plus 30-day DAPT; major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 22.6% vs 29% (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.57-0.98, p=0.033), driven by lower myocardial infarction (3.5% vs 10.4%) and target vessel revascularization (5.9% vs 11.4%) with E-ZES.
Stent thrombosis was significantly reduced with E-ZES, while bleeding events did not differ between stent groups.
These findings do not support BMS implantation as justifiable in HBR patients when a suitable drug-eluting stent can be used with abbreviated DAPT.
No—septoplasty did not significantly change the dimensions of compensatory middle turbinate hypertrophy in patients with nasal septal deviation.

In these patients, bony and mucosal middle turbinate dimensions on the concave and convex sides of the septum were measured radiologically before septoplasty and at least one year after, and no significant changes were found by paired sample t-test or Wilcoxon rank sum test.

There was, however, a significant negative correlation after septoplasty between the angle of the septum and the middle turbinate total area on the deviated side (p = 0.033), which does not establish a change in dimensions.
No; the study shows paucigranulocytic asthmatics are not truly non-inflammatory.

In a retrospective cross-sectional study of 833 asthmatics compared with 194 healthy subjects, sputum eosinophils (absolute and percentage) were increased in all asthma phenotypes including paucigranulocytic asthma versus healthy subjects (p < 0.005).
All asthma phenotypes also had increased blood leukocyte counts versus healthy subjects, and paucigranulocytic asthmatics specifically had increased absolute blood eosinophils (p < 0.005).

Thus, although total sputum non-squamous cell counts were greater in mixed granulocytic and neutrophilic phenotypes than in paucigranulocytic asthma (p < 0.005), the paucigranulocytic group still shows local and systemic inflammatory markers above healthy controls.
The evidence is insufficient to establish obesity as the triggering cause of incidentally detected idiopathic misty mesentery, although the study reports a high obesity prevalence in this population.

Among 561 patients with misty mesentery on abdominopelvic CT, 80 had isolated incidental idiopathic misty mesentery, a prevalence of 7%, and 67.5% of all patients were obese while 17.5% were overweight.
The study excluded known causes and described CT findings but did not include a control group or analysis testing whether obesity causes the condition.
The evidence is mixed: LAA occlusion altered some ECG parameters but not immediate echocardiographic parameters in patients with AF.

In 73 patients undergoing Watchman, LAmbre, or Lefort implantation, there was a slight measurable QRS axis movement in most patients and significant pre- vs post-operative differences in heart rate and mean-mean QT interval.

Echocardiographic parameters showed no significant difference immediately before vs after device implantation, but LA diameter was larger at 6-month follow-up and aortic root diameter was larger at 12-month follow-up than pre-operation baseline.
No, viral co-infection did not influence the severity of acute respiratory infection in children; the number of detected viruses did not correlate with any markers of severity.
This finding came from 204 children admitted with acute respiratory infection in a Spanish prospective multicenter study (2011-2013) and was replicated in an independent UK cohort of 97 children.

In contrast, bacterial superinfection was associated with increased severity (OR 4.356, P=0.005), PICU admission (OR 3.342, P=0.006), higher clinical score (1.988, P=0.002), respiratory support (OR 7.484, P<0.001), and longer hospital length of stay (OR 1.468, P<0.001).
The evidence is insufficient to say whether rectal anastomosis in gynaecological debulking surgery is safe without a diverting stoma.

In a retrospective series, 43 major colorectal procedures were performed on 37 women, most commonly low rectal resection (n = 22; 59%), anterior rectal resection (n = 7; 19%), and sigmoid resection (n = 4; 11%).
Only 3 patients (8%) received a diverting loop ileostomy, and 5 (14%) underwent Hartmann's procedure.
The passages state that anastomotic leakage was the primary outcome but do not report leakage rates by presence or absence of a diverting stoma, so they do not settle the safety question.
The evidence is mixed: infectious disease doctors agree moderately on appropriate antimicrobial prescribing, but not completely.

In 24 infectious disease or clinical microbiology doctors (16 specialists and 8 residents) from five hospitals assessing 56 paper cases, specialists agreed with a modal expert reference standard in 80% of cases (range 75%-86%), with sensitivity 75% and specificity 84%.
Specialists agreed with an index expert in 76% of cases, while the index expert agreed with his own previous assessments in 71% of cases.
These findings show substantial but imperfect agreement, so expert assessment is not fully consistent.

Yes, flexible instruments can create adequate femoral tunnel lengths at 90° of knee flexion in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, based on a cadaveric study finding a mean intra-osseous length of 32.1 mm at 90°. In 10 fresh cadaveric knees, flexible guide pins were inserted at 70°, 90°, and 120° of flexion, and intra-osseous length was measured. The mean intra-osseous length at 90° was 32.1 mm (range 22–45 mm), which exceeds the 20 mm adequacy threshold and was significantly greater than the 70° mean of 25.2 mm (range 20–32 mm; p<0.05). There were no significant differences among flexion groups in distance to the lateral collateral ligament.
The evidence is mixed: KIT mutation analysis may help identify likely responders to neoadjuvant imatinib, but it did not account for all outcome differences in locally advanced GIST.

Among 125 patients with locally advanced or locally recurrent GIST treated with neoadjuvant imatinib, only 45 (36%) had c-kit mutation testing; exon 11 was found in 25 (55.5%), exon 9 in 3 (6.7%), exon 13 in 2 (4.4%), wild type in 12 (26.6%), and 3 (6.7%) were uninterpretable.
Exon 11 mutants had a higher response rate than non-exon 11 mutants (84% vs 40%, p=0.01), and disease stabilization rates were 92% vs 75%, respectively.

However, there were no differences between the various exon variants in outcomes and responses, and the introduction states that longer neoadjuvant imatinib duration is not based on tumor biology reflected by kit mutation analysis.
No, there is no significant correlation between humeral and glenoidal bony lesions in chronic anterior posttraumatic shoulder dislocation.

In a retrospective study of 30 patients with chronic posttraumatic anterior shoulder instability and bone defects in both the glenoid and humerus, the mean D/R was 23 ± 12% and 23 ± 10% and mean D1/D2 was 95 ± 4% and 94 ± 6% for two observers.
No significant correlation was found between humeral and glenoid bone defects by observer 1 (r = 0.23, p = 0.22) or observer 2 (r = 0.05, p = 0.78).
No—risk calculators did not accurately predict surgical site occurrence (SSO) in this study.

In patients undergoing open ventral hernia repair followed for at least 1 month, across a retrospective multicenter database (n=795; SSO rate 23%) and a single-center prospective database (n=88; SSO rate 14%), the tested models (VHRS, VHWG, CDC Wound Class, HW-RAT, and, in the prospective cohort, ACS-NSQIP) had low AUCs for SSO, ranging from 0.50 to 0.60 in the retrospective database and 0.50 to 0.69 in the prospective database.

Although VHRS and HW-RAT significantly stratified SSO in the retrospective database and ACS-NSQIP did so in the prospective database, the models also systematically over- or underestimated SSO risk, so the passages show limited accuracy rather than reliable prediction.
Yes, electrochemiluminescence (ECL) assays improved prediction of time to type 1 diabetes in autoantibody-positive TrialNet subjects.

In 1,287 TrialNet subjects positive for one or more autoantibodies (microinsulin autoantibody, GAD65 autoantibody, IA-2A, and/or ZnT8A) with ECL-IAA and ECL-GADA data at baseline, 177 developed diabetes after a median 24 months.

ECL-positive subjects had a 6-year risk of progression of 58% versus 5% in ECL-negative subjects (P<0.0001), and in multivariate Cox models the model including ECL-GADA and/or ECL-IAA positivity was best, with ECL positivity remaining significantly associated with time to diabetes.
Adding ECL to the Diabetes Prevention Trial risk score improved the receiver operating characteristic curves with an AUC of 0.83 (P<0.0001).
Yes—qualitative findings suggest MPH programs can contribute to health system strengthening in low- and middle-income countries, mainly through workplace and policy impacts.

In a six-country mixed-methods study focused on two English-language MPH programs (a distance program from South Africa and a residential program in the Netherlands), 10 graduates per program working in low- and middle-income health systems, plus their peers and supervisors, reported considerable workplace impact.

Reported contributions included promotion to leadership positions, expanded or revitalized management roles, workplace innovations, teaching and training, advocacy, community engagement, and national-level policy advisory roles, policy development, and capacity building.
However, these findings are qualitative and context-dependent, with work conditions influencing impact and possible self-selection, untraceable graduates, and social acceptability bias.

Evidence is mixed: familial drinking patterns show some persistence into young adulthood, but mainly as a difference between abstaining and non-abstaining families rather than a graded transmission of drinking levels.

In a Swedish longitudinal study (n=744), young adults from families that were abstainers in 2000 drank substantially less across quintiles in 2010 than offspring of non-abstaining families, though the difference was not statistically significant between quintiles of the conditional distribution.
Actual drinking levels in drinking families were not at all or weakly associated with offspring drinking, and supplementary analyses confirmed these patterns.
Yes—multimodal cervical physical therapy improved tinnitus in patients with cervicogenic somatic tinnitus, with significant TFI reduction after treatment.

In a randomized controlled trial of 38 patients with severe subjective tinnitus (TFI 25–90) and neck complaints (NBQ >14), all received cervical physical therapy for 6 weeks (12 sessions) in either an immediate-start or 6-week delayed-start group.

After treatment, TFI and NBQ scores decreased significantly (p = 0.04 and p < 0.001), and 53% reported substantial tinnitus improvement immediately, though only 24% maintained that effect at 6-week follow-up.
No; in children with anisometropic hyperopic unilateral amblyopia, six months of amblyopia treatment did not normalize subfoveal choroidal thickness.

In 32 such children treated with full refractive correction, refractive adaptation, and fellow-eye patching, the mean choroidal thickness was significantly higher in amblyopic than fellow eyes at baseline (p=0.019).
There was no significant pre- to post-treatment change in amblyopic eyes (p=0.428) or fellow eyes (p=0.343).
After treatment, choroidal thickness remained significantly higher in amblyopic than fellow eyes (p=0.006), even though visual acuity improved.
The evidence is mixed: adolescent comorbid MD/AUD is associated with poorer adult depression outcomes in unadjusted analyses, but after adjustment it no longer differs significantly from MD-only.

In longitudinal data from ages 15-18 to 18-35, the comorbid MD/AUD group had significantly (p<.05) higher rates of adult MD than the AUD-only group and marginally (p<.10) higher rates than the MD-only group, while all three disorder groups had significantly (p<.05) higher rates than the no-disorder group.

After adjustment for confounding, however, the difference in adult MD rates between the MD-only and MD/AUD groups was no longer statistically significant; gender, childhood behavior problems, and physical/sexual abuse explained the associations.
Thus the passages show an association but do not establish that comorbidity itself leads to poorer depression outcomes.
The data were self-report and may have been subject to biases.
Yes—the retromandibular transparotid approach appeared safe and reliable for surgical treatment of condylar fractures in a retrospective series of 25 patients.
In that study, preinjury occlusion and temporomandibular joint health were restored in most patients, and esthetic outcomes were satisfactory to clinicians and patients.
Neither permanent neurologic impairments nor major postoperative complications were observed.
However, this was a single retrospective evaluation without a stated comparator, so it supports reliability but does not definitively compare the approach with others.
The passages do not settle whether the Catholic bishops' boycott call affected polio vaccination coverage in Kenya in 2015.

They show national coverage was 93% in August 2015 compared with 94% in November 2014, and parental refusal as a reason for missed vaccination increased from 6% to 12%, but they do not directly attribute these changes to the boycott.
Catholic parents/guardians were 31% of the sample but only 7% of missed children, and the survey sampled 90,157 children and 37,732 parents/guardians across 32 counties.

Yes, the evidence suggests that aortic arch anatomy influences aortic trauma severity, with the aortic arch angle significantly associated with type III damage in a retrospective series. That study included 22 patients treated with TEVAR for traumatic aortic injury from 2009 to 2014 and classified injury severity according to Society of Vascular Surgery recommendations. Mean aortic arch index and angle were 6.8 cm and 58.3° for type I, 4.4 cm and 45.9° for type III, and 3.3 cm and 37° for type IV, with substantial differences between type III and IV groups. Multivariate analysis confirmed the aortic arch angle was significantly associated with type III damage (OR 1.5; 95% CI 1.03-2.2). However, these findings come from only 22 cases in one department, so they are limited.
No—simultaneous neuroendoscope use during ventriculoperitoneal shunt procedures did not significantly influence the incidence of shunt infection in the supplied study.
Among 438 VPS procedures, infection occurred in 22.4% when an endoscope was used versus 18% when it was not (P = 0.449).
In first-time shunt insertions, infection rates were 28.6% with endoscope vs 16.2% without (P = 0.27), and in revised or second-time insertions they were 20% vs 19.8% (P = 0.977).
These results do not show a statistically significant increase or decrease in infection associated with endoscope use.

Yes, the supplied evidence indicates that strategically used performance measurement systems (PMS) are useful, because strategic use of PMS directly and significantly (p < 0.001) enhanced performance in terms of improved processes in health care organizations.
This rests on a PLS analysis of a survey of 97 Italian managers working in Lombardy health care organizations, with a 77.6% response rate.
The relevant comparison is strategic versus non-strategic use of PMS, with prior literature suggesting strategic use enhances quality.
Perceived managerial discretion was also positively and significantly affected by strategic PMS use (p < 0.001), while the mediation effect was non-significant.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that non-HDL-C is a better predictor of long-term outcome after AMI than LDL-C.

In 868 Thai patients after AMI followed for 2.6 ± 1.6 years, non-HDL-C >130 mg/dl was associated with higher MACE versus non-HDL-C <100 mg/dl (HR 3.15, 95% CI 1.46-6.80, P=0.003), whereas LDL-C >100 mg/dl was unexpectedly associated with lower MACE versus LDL-C <70 mg/dl (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.18-0.98, P=0.046) after direct pairwise comparison with non-HDL-C.
The study directly compared LDL-C and non-HDL-C in a Cox model, but the supplied results do not report a head-to-head discrimination statistic showing non-HDL-C is superior.
No, the passage indicates sub-Saharan Africa is not yet ready to cope with the increased ART-related adverse effects expected from the WHO "test and treat" policy.

In sub-Saharan Africa, implementing the WHO test-and-treat policy is expected to exacerbate ART-related adverse effects such as cardiovascular disease, lipodystrophy, prediabetes and overt diabetes, insulin resistance, and hyperlactatemia/lactic acidosis, whose prevalence is already high.

The region faces extreme poverty, weak health systems, inadequate health services, lack of qualified personnel and equipment, unaffordable medicines, heavy workload, and a dearth of data on ART-related adverse effect incidence and predictive factors, with no quantitative estimates provided in the passage.
These gaps mean the region cannot adequately anticipate, prevent, or respond to the upcoming burden without additional data and preparation.

The evidence is insufficient to conclude that healthier lifestyles lead to less healthcare utilization; the supplied study reports only that four health behaviors were significantly correlated with healthcare utilization (P<0.05). In 2,911 people older than 15 surveyed in Kaohsiung, Taiwan in 2005, exercise habits, dietary habits, regular blood pressure measurement, and drinking habits were each significantly associated with healthcare utilization. The regression models also showed significant correlations for doctor-visit frequency, health examinations, and seeking the same physician with gender, age, and education, but the passages do not report the direction or magnitude of the health-behavior associations.
Yes, the evidence indicates that the first urinary ACR has prognostic value for both maternal and neonatal composite adverse outcomes in women with suspected preeclampsia.

In a retrospective cohort of 717 pregnant women with singleton pregnancies after 20 weeks' gestation referred for suspected preeclampsia, a 1-unit increase in log-transformed ACR was associated with increased odds of adverse maternal outcome (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.45-1.80) and adverse neonatal outcome (OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.02-1.29), and with reduced gestational age at delivery (coefficient -0.46, 95% CI -0.54 to -0.38).
These associations came from multivariable logistic regression adjusting for existing prognostic factors, supporting independent prognostic value.
Yes, a single-level VAT area can represent VAT volume changes, based on the strongest correlation at a slice 3 cm above the lower margin of L3 (r=0.853).
This rests on 60 abdominal CT images from 30 males (mean age 51 years) scanned twice within 1 year, comparing VAT areas at various levels with VAT volume and body weight changes.
At that slice, VAT area also correlated strongly with body weight change (r=0.902).
The passages show this for changes in VAT volume, not for absolute VAT volume.

Yes, the evidence suggests that the distance to a high-volume center is worth it for rectal cancer resection, because long-distance/high-volume care was associated with better outcomes than short-distance/low-volume care. In a population-based National Cancer Database study of 18,605 patients with stage II or III rectal cancer who underwent surgical resection between 2006 and 2012, the long-distance/high-volume group (n=2067; median travel 62.6 miles) was compared with the short-distance/low-volume group (n=1362; median travel 2.3 miles). After adjustment, the short-distance/low-volume group had lower odds of lymph node yield ≥12 (OR=0.51) and neoadjuvant chemoradiation (OR=0.67), higher 30-day (OR=3.38) and 90-day mortality (OR=2.07), and a 34% higher risk of overall mortality at 5 years compared with the long-distance/high-volume group. However, the study lacked data on patient and physician decision making and surgeon-specific factors, so residual confounding cannot be excluded.

The evidence is insufficient to definitively say cardiopulmonary bypass temperature does not affect postoperative euthyroid sick syndrome, although one small study found similar thyroid hormone changes in warm and cold CPB.
In 12 cardiac surgery patients, 6 had normothermic (35±1°C) and 6 hypothermic (26±5°C) CPB.
Both groups showed reduced TT4 and TT3 for up to 5 days, reduced free T3 for up to 3 days, elevated rT3 on postoperative days 1 and 3, and unchanged TSH.
However, the passages do not report a direct between-group statistical comparison of these thyroid outcomes, so they do not conclusively show that temperature has no effect.
No, continuous intravenous infusion of low-concentration epinephrine did not impair uterine blood flow in pregnant ewes.

In 10 near-term gravid ewes, infusions of saline, 0.125% bupivacaine alone, and 0.125% bupivacaine with epinephrine at 1:200,000, 1:400,000, or 1:800,000 had no effect on any measured hemodynamic variable, including uterine blood flow.
In contrast, a bolus intravenous injection of epinephrine 15 micrograms decreased uterine blood flow to 68 +/- 14% of baseline.

The evidence is insufficient to establish hyperbaric oxygenation (HBO) as an indication for necrotizing fasciitis, because this retrospective comparison found no mortality benefit and more débridements with HBO.
Among 37 patients treated from 1984–1993, 25 received HBO plus surgery/antibiotics and 12 received surgery/antibiotics alone.

Mortality was 36% in the HBO group versus 25% in the non-HBO group, and the mean number of surgical débridements was significantly higher with HBO (3.3 vs 1.5); hospitalization for survivors was shorter with HBO but not statistically significant.

No, earlier discharge from Winnipeg hospitals did not appear to adversely affect quality of care in this study, as length of stay fell significantly without consistent increases in readmission rates or physician visits.

In Manitoba residents admitted to seven large acute care Winnipeg hospitals for acute myocardial infarction (AMI), bronchitis or asthma, transurethral prostatectomy (TURP), or uterine/adnexal procedures from 1989-90 to 1992-93, length of stay decreased significantly for all four categories, from 11.1% for AMI to 22.0% for bronchitis or asthma.

Readmission rates showed no consistent change for AMI, bronchitis or asthma, and TURP; the uterine/adnexal readmission rate increased significantly between the first and second year (chi2=4.28, p=0.04) but then remained constant, and mean physician visits increased slightly for AMI (1.92 to 2.01) then stayed virtually the same and decreased slightly for bronchitis or asthma.

There was no significant correlation between length of stay and readmission rates for individual hospitals in 1992-93 in any of the four categories, nor between length of stay and mean physician visits for AMI and bronchitis or asthma.

Yes—30-day data appear sufficient for measuring hospital mortality, because 30-day postadmission mortality discriminated the top and bottom fifths of 180-day mortality extremely well, especially for AMI.

This finding rests on FY 1989 HCFA hospital mortality data for all Medicare patients and patients in three cardiac categories: coronary artery bypass graft surgery, acute myocardial infarction, and congestive heart failure.
The comparison used 0–30, 31–180, and 0–180-day postadmission mortality; 31–180-day data corroborated the 0–30-day results, though cross-condition correlations were weaker in the 31–180-day interval.

The evidence is mixed or limited on whether ultrasound is a useful addition to clinical staging in penile squamous cell carcinoma. In 16 patients with primary tumors and 1 with recurrent cancer, ultrasound identified all tumors as hypoechoic and clearly demonstrated absence or presence of invasion into the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum when compared with histopathology. However, ultrasound could not differentiate subepithelial tissue invasion from corpus spongiosum invasion, and it accurately measured maximum tumor thickness in only 7 of 16 examinations. Thus the passages show selective staging value but do not settle overall clinical utility.

The evidence is insufficient to say whether physicians are meeting the needs of family caregivers of frail elderly, because the supplied study assessed caregiver needs and dissatisfaction with the health care system rather than physician performance specifically.

In a volunteer sample of caregivers in the Montreal Jewish community caring for someone 60 or older, an average of 75.4% did not use formal support services, just under half were dissatisfied with the attention they received from the health care system, and more than one third reported stress, depression, guilt, and isolation.
These findings show substantial caregiver need and some health-system dissatisfaction, but they do not isolate whether physicians met those needs.
Yes, breast-feeding was associated with lower childhood illness rates in children with a family history of atopy.

In a historic cohort of 794 children with a family history of atopy, breast-fed children had fewer episodes of gastroenteritis, lower respiratory tract infections, and digestive tract disorders in the first year of life, and fewer respiratory tract infections and skin infections over the next three years, compared with non-breast-fed children.
However, this cohort study shows an association, not proof that breast-feeding is best.

The evidence is mixed/limited: in non-insulin-dependent diabetic (NIDDM) subjects the insertion (II) genotype was associated with insulin resistance compared with the deletion (DD) genotype, but no such association was seen in nondiabetic subjects.

Among 103 NIDDM subjects, those with DD had lower specific insulin than ID and II (DD 38.6, ID 57.1, II 87.4 pmol/L, ANOVA P=.011), and non-insulin-treated DD subjects had greater insulin sensitivity by HOMA % than II subjects (DD 56.4% vs II 29.4%, P=.027) and lower des 31,32 proinsulin (DD 3.3 vs II 7.6 pmol/L, P=.012).
In 533 nondiabetic white subjects, there were no differences in insulin sensitivity, insulin-like molecules, blood pressure, PAI-1, serum lipids, or CHD prevalence across ACE genotypes.
Thus the supplied data do not establish the insertion allele as a consistent candidate for insulin resistance; they show a possible association only in NIDDM subjects.
No, the supplied evidence does not support serovar-specific immunity to Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

In 508 episodes of gonorrhoea, including 22 patients with multiple infections over 4 years, no significant difference was seen in the prevalence of serovars isolated following a repeat infection compared with those without repeat infections, and the site of initial infection did not appear to influence the subsequent serovar isolated.
The study was designed to test whether the host immune response provides limited serovar-specific protection from reinfection, but these results suggest it does not.

The evidence is mixed: a slightly elevated risk of diabetes was found among glassworks employees (MH-OR 1.2, 95% CI 0.82-1.8) and in workers probably exposed to arsenic (MH-OR 1.4, 95% CI 0.92-2.2), with a higher risk in unspecified glass workers likely highly exposed (MH-OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1-2.8).
This came from a case-referent analysis of 5498 death records in the art glass producing part of southeastern Sweden, including 888 glass workers.

Because most confidence intervals included 1.0, the passages do not establish that diabetes was caused by arsenic exposure, though the high-exposure subgroup finding is compatible with such an effect.
The evidence is mixed or insufficient to conclude that marginally acceptable hearts are suitable for transplantation.

In 55 potential brain-dead donors evaluated by TEE, 20 had FAC <50%, and 40 hearts were harvested, 36 successfully transplanted; among recipients, 9 had donor FAC <50% (group H2) and 27 had donor FAC >50% (group H1).

Four recipients died, including one from right and one from left ventricular dysfunction with donor FAC <50%, while donor FAC increased from 51 +/- 15% to 57 +/- 11% in 18 hearts assessed in donors and later recipients.

Actuarial survival was 86.2% versus 64.6% at 1 and 2 years in group H1 versus group H2, respectively, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = NS), so these data do not definitively settle suitability.

No, the supplied results weigh against well-differentiated small HCC being clinically early cancer, because there was no significant difference in disease-free survival between well-differentiated and less-differentiated tumors and tumor-volume-doubling-time analysis of recurrent foci suggested minute cancerous foci were already present at operation.
In 76 patients with solitary small HCCs up to 3 cm who underwent hepatectomy and were observed for at least 2 years, 10 had well-differentiated grade I HCC and 66 had less-differentiated HCC.

Well-differentiated HCC had lower fibrous capsule formation (P<0.01), but there were no significant differences in intrahepatic metastasis, portal vein invasion, or disease-free survival, and microscopic cancer-cell infiltration into the fibrous frame of the portal tract was present.
Yes, socioeconomic differences in mortality persist after retirement, though the relative predictive strength of employment grade declines.

In 18,133 male civil servants aged 40-69 followed for 25 years, the lowest employment grade had 3.12 times the mortality of the highest before retirement (95% CI 2.4 to 4.1), and this fell to a rate ratio of 1.86 (1.6 to 2.2) after retirement.

A non-work measure, car ownership, predicted mortality less well before retirement but declined less after retirement, and employment grade and car ownership had independent associations of equal magnitude after retirement.
The absolute difference in death rates between lowest and highest grades increased with age from 12.9 per 1000 person years at ages 40-64 to 38.3 per 1000 at ages 70-89.
The evidence is mixed: pediatric housestaff experience was associated with more arterial blood gases ordered but not with radiographs or electrolytes.

In a prospective cohort of all 785 infants admitted to one academic Level III neonatal ICU over one academic year, cared for by 14 categorical pediatric housestaff, interns ordered significantly more arterial blood gases per infant than residents (3.22 vs.
2.89 per call night, p =.02), amounting to 0.33 more per infant per call night, after controlling for severity of illness, workload, and supervision.
However, there was no difference between interns and residents in ordering radiographs or electrolytes.

The evidence is mixed/limited: FNA cytology identified only one significantly different feature, a swirling epithelial pattern, but it does not cleanly distinguish nonproliferative breast disease (NPBD) from proliferative breast disease without atypia (PBD).
In 51 air-dried Diff-Quik FNA samples from palpable breast lesions with biopsy-proven diagnoses, a swirling pattern occurred in 13/17 PBD cases (76%) versus 12/34 NPBD cases (35%) (P = 0.008).
This was the only cytologic feature significantly different among those evaluated, and reported criteria for this distinction had not been rigorously tested.
Thus, the passages show a statistical association but not a reliable cytologic separation.

No, gestational age misclassification does not appear to explain the difference in birthweights between Australian Aborigines and whites; only extreme types of misclassification removed the divergence in median birthweights.

In the study, after 34 weeks gestation, birthweight means and centiles increased more slowly for Australian Aborigines than for whites, and simulations tested whether differential misclassification of gestational age caused this pattern.

At full term, birthweight distribution parameters were robust to gestational age misclassification, and at preterm the 10th centiles were robust, though 90th centiles were sensitive to even minor misclassification.

Thus, the passages indicate that misclassification does not explain the Aboriginal-white difference except under implausible extreme assumptions, but they do not provide a specific numeric effect size for the difference.

The evidence is mixed or insufficient: no clear effect on conception was found, but the passages do not address pregnancy outcomes. The study retrospectively compared 270 infertile couples with a pair-matched control fertile population for occupational ionizing radiation exposure in a nuclear power plant. It found no differences in the frequency of nuclear power plant exposure between the sterile and fertile groups. However, nuclear power plant workers had a higher rate of anomalous spermiograms, although the abnormalities were temporary. No correlation was found between cumulative equivalent radiation dose and abnormal spermiograms.
Yes, the evidence supports VLEM as a true endoscopic manifestation of esophagitis in children, though the passages describe esophageal mucosa generally rather than specifically distal mucosa.

In a review of 255 esophageal biopsies, histology was normal in only 1 of 41 children whose sole mucosal abnormality was VLEM (2.4%), compared with 92 of 160 children with normal-appearing mucosa (57.5%).
Most children with VLEM had eosinophilic esophagitis (34/41, 83%; specificity 0.85, sensitivity 0.50), often moderate to severe (31/34, 91.2%; specificity 0.88, sensitivity 0.73).

Yes, endothelial/vascular patterns of astrocytomas appear indicative of grade, based on a study of 17 astrocytoma surgical specimens (7 pediatric, 10 adult) and 4 normal autopsy brains evaluated with GFAP and von Willebrand factor by confocal microscopy.

Pilocytic astrocytomas (4 cases) showed lacy clusters of small-to-medium vessels with intact vessel wall integrity, while diffuse low-grade astrocytomas (3 cases) showed a pattern similar to control tissue.

In contrast, intermediate-grade (1 case), anaplastic astrocytoma (3 cases), and glioblastoma multiforme (6 cases) showed increased vessel density with glomeruloid clusters, some with intimal hyperplasia, loss of vessel wall integrity, and numerous vWF-positive single cells/microvessels within the tumor substance.
Thus, higher-grade tumors had more abnormal endothelial/vascular patterns than lower-grade tumors and controls.
The evidence is insufficient to conclude that MRI can substitute for diagnostic arthroscopy in occult posttraumatic knee lesions.

In 70 patients with acute trauma, negative radiographs, pain, and limited movement, MRI identified bone bruises (n=25), subchondral (n=33), and osteochondral (n=35) injuries, while arthroscopy depicted 45 osteochondral and 19 chondral injuries.

The study defined MRI signal patterns for bone bruises and noted osteochondral injuries had associated bone and cartilage damage, but it did not report comparative accuracy or agreement between MRI and arthroscopy.
Therefore, the passages show MRI can detect and characterize such lesions but do not establish that it can replace arthroscopy.

No—in this small randomized trial, paracervical block did not demonstrate additional advantages during second-trimester abortion induction with gemeprost. The study included 20 women at 16–23 weeks who received 1 mg gemeprost vaginally every 6 hours and were randomized to Pethidin/Butylscopolamine alone (n=10) or plus paracervical anaesthesia (n=10). Median induction-to-abortion interval was 20 hours (range 8–44) without versus 13 hours (range 8–36) with paracervical anaesthesia, which was not statistically significant. Pain intensity and Pethidin requirement did not differ significantly, while Butylscopolamine requirement was higher in the paracervical group (p<0.05). Thus, the available evidence from this small study does not show additional benefit, though it is limited by the very small sample size.
No—successful completion of the Perinatal Education Programme did not result in improved obstetric practice in this study, although all completing midwives improved in knowledge.

In a Mpumalanga health district, 8 of 13 midwives at two midwife obstetric units completed PEP while a third unit did not, and before-and-after scoring of 303 patient obstetric files found no change in referral patterns and no differences before or after PEP in syphilis testing (56–82%), haemoglobin measurement (4–15%), or response to detected uterine growth problems (0–8%).

Appropriate action for detected antenatal problems remained unsatisfactory (0–12%), and although appropriate intrapartum actions improved where problems were detected, the improvement was not significant.
No, the SCL 90-R obsessive-compulsive subscale did not identify objective cognitive impairments in adults with malignant brain tumors.
In 19 adults assessed before aggressive chemotherapy, the subscale was not related to objective measures of attention, verbal memory, or age.
